documents.abstract: This study investigates how digital financial literacy, perceived transparency of artificial intelligence advisory services, investment and wealth knowledge, and cyber-risk self-protection shape Perceived Private Wealth Management Capability (PWMC) among digitally engaged retail investors in an emerging-market context. PWMC is conceptualized as a self-assessed capability outcome rather than an objective indicator of wealth-management performance, portfolio returns, or private-banking status. Drawing on the financial capability framework, trust in automation theory, and protection motivation theory, the study develops a trust-to-capability model in which trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory and digital wealth management behavior serves as a key explanatory mechanism. A non-probability sample of 249 digitally engaged retail investors in Vietnam was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling in SmartPLS 4.1, with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. The results show that digital financial literacy is the strongest antecedent of trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory (β = 0.517, p < 0.001). At the same time, perceived advisory transparency also exerts a significant positive effect (β = 0.261, p < 0.001). Investment and wealth knowledge emerged as the strongest predictor of digital wealth management behavior (β = 0.348, p < 0.001). Trust, digital wealth management behavior, and investment and wealth knowledge each positively influence perceived private wealth management capability. Digital wealth management behavior partially mediates the effects of trust, investment, and wealth knowledge on perceived capability. Cyber-risk self-protection limited evidence of a boundary condition by strengthening the relationship between trust and digital wealth management behavior. However, the effect size is small and should be interpreted cautiously (β = 0.098, p = 0.038). The model explains 60.2% of the variance in digital wealth management behavior and 44.3% of the variance in perceived private wealth management capability. By moving beyond conventional explanations of robo-advisory adoption and technology acceptance, this study theorizes hybrid AI advisory as a calibrated trust environment in which retail investors’ perceived capability depends not only on whether they trust AI-supported advice but also on whether that trust translates into protective, enacted digital wealth management behavior. The findings should be interpreted in the context of digitally engaged retail investors. They should not be generalized to private banking clients, high-net-worth investors, objective portfolio performance, or verified wealth outcomes.

This article examines the evolving landscape of digital human rights, with particular focus on personal data privacy and the emerging threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on international legal frameworks — including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — the article analyses the gap between existing legal protections and the rapidly advancing digital ecosystem. Through doctrinal legal analysis and a comparative case study methodology, the research identifies key vulnerabilities in current data protection regimes and evaluates institutional responses at the international, regional, and national levels. The findings demonstrate that while significant legal infrastructure exists, enforcement remains inconsistent and AI-specific regulation is still nascent. The article concludes with policy recommendations aimed at strengthening digital rights protection frameworks, with particular reference to Uzbekistan.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose: This paper analyses how digital tools such as artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and digital twin technologies can enhance risk assessment and decision-making in business operations. Design/Methodology/Approach: The research studies the existing literature on digital transformation and risk management, drawing on 29 publications from 2020 to 2026 (27 journal articles published in the Scopus database and two book chapters). The publications are analysed using thematic synthesis based on three constructs: digital tools, risk assessment capability, and decision-making performance. Research Limitation: The study is based on existing literature, indicating the need for further research on the practical implementation of digital technologies in different business environments. Findings: The results suggest that introducing digital technologies into management systems speeds decision-making, improves risk management, and makes organisations more competitive. Digital technologies enable organisations to process large amounts of real-time data, detect potential risks, and support more informed, timely managerial decisions. Practical Implication: The findings show that digital tools can improve risk assessment procedures and support more effective managerial decision-making. Social Implication: More efficient decision-making and risk management contribute to greater organisational resilience in dynamic business environments. Originality/Value: The study addresses two gaps in the literature: insufficient analysis of technology combinations and the human factor. In its tool-to-capability framework, digital tools contribute to operational performance indirectly by affecting risk assessment and decision-making, an effect the synthesis links to governance and managerial competencies.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation is changing the way banks and financial institutions work. It affects how they process payments, manage investments, check transactions, protect customer data and meet regulatory rules. Banks now use digital platforms, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud systems and data analytics to improve speed, accuracy and control across their operations. This change is important for international banking. A single financial transaction can involve clients, banks, payment networks, regulators and service providers in different countries. Each party must share accurate information and complete its task within the required time. Digital systems help connect these activities and reduce manual work. Mumbai is a major financial centre in India. It has domestic and international banks, investment firms, stock exchanges and financial service companies. As these organisations adopt new technology, the need for professionals who understand both finance and digital operations is also changing. Global & Investment Banking Operations in Mumbai is therefore a relevant field for people who want to build careers at the meeting point of banking, investment services and technology. The Main Drivers of Digital Transformation Several factors are pushing financial institutions to update their systems and processes. 1. Faster financial transactions Customers and businesses expect payments and transfers to move quickly. Banks must process high volumes of transactions while keeping records accurate. Digital payment platforms and automated workflows help reduce delays and manual work. 2. Stronger risk controls Banks must identify suspicious activity, prevent fraud and protect customer information. Digital monitoring systems can review large volumes of data and flag unusual activity for further checks. 3. Better customer service Digital platforms allow customers to access account information, submit documents and track requests. Banks can use data analytics to understand customer needs and improve service. 4. Global business operations International banks work across countries, currencies and time zones. Connected systems help teams share transaction details, process instructions and manage records across different locations. These changes are influencing Global & Investment Banking Operations in Mumbai. Financial institutions need teams that understand both the financial process and the technology that supports it. Key Technologies Changing Banking Operations Digital transformation does not depend on one tool. It involves a group of technologies that work together. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning AI can help banks review documents, detect unusual transactions, classify service requests and support risk analysis. Machine learning systems can study patterns in data and identify activity that may need attention. A September 2026 report covered by The Economic Times found that Indian financial institutions are using AI in areas such as underwriting, fraud management, collections, compliance and customer service. It also noted that firms face challenges when they try to scale AI because of fragmented data, integration needs, security and governance. <Cite refs={["turn215787view1"]}/> AI can support banking employees, but it does not remove the need for human review. Staff must check important decisions, handle complex cases and make sure that the system follows approved rules. Cloud Computing Cloud systems allow banks to store and process data through connected digital infrastructure. They can support flexible access, faster system updates and better coordination between departments. A report published by The Economic Times CFO in October 2026 described the growing use of AI, cloud and connected enterprise systems across India's NBFC and BFSI sector. It also highlighted issues such as legacy systems, fragmented data and regulatory requirements. For Global & Investment Banking Operations in Mumbai, cloud knowledge can be useful because international financial institutions often need secure systems that support teams across different locations. Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) APIs allow different software systems to exchange information. Banks use them to connect payment platforms, customer applications, financial data systems and service providers. For example, an API can help transfer payment instructions from one system to another. It can also support account verification and data sharing between approved platforms. Strong API security is important. Poor access controls can expose systems to unauthorised activity. Robotic Process Automation Robotic Process Automation (RPA) uses software bots to perform rule-based tasks. These tasks may include data entry, report preparation, record matching and document movement. RPA can reduce repetitive work and help teams complete standard tasks with greater speed. Employees can then focus on exceptions, quality checks and more complex cases. Data Analytics and Business Intelligence Banks use data analytics to study transaction volumes, customer activity, investment performance and operational errors. Dashboards can help managers monitor key measures and identify problems. Tools such as advanced Excel and Looker Studio can support reporting and data presentation. Professionals who can convert financial data into clear reports can add value to operations teams. Digital Transformation Across Banking Functions Digital systems affect many parts of banking. Each function has its own processes, risks and technology needs. Payments and Cross-Border Transfers International payments can involve several banks and payment networks. Teams must check payment details, currency information, beneficiary records and compliance requirements. Digital payment systems can improve the speed and visibility of these processes. However, banks must still follow rules for identity checks, sanctions screening and transaction monitoring. Trade Finance Operations Trade finance supports international trade through products such as letters of credit, bank guarantees and documentary collections. These processes involve several documents and parties. Digital document systems can help teams store, review and share trade records. Automated checks can also identify missing information or differences in documents. Investment and Securities Operations Investment operations support the processing of financial products such as shares, bonds and derivatives. They include trade confirmation, clearing, settlement, reconciliation and corporate actions. Digital platforms help teams track trade details and monitor transaction status. Accurate data is essential because errors can affect client accounts and financial records. KYC and Anti-Money Laundering Know Your Customer (KYC) checks help banks confirm the identity of clients. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) controls help detect and report activity that may involve illegal funds. Digital identity checks, document review tools and transaction monitoring systems can support these activities. Employees must still review alerts and follow the correct escalation process. Cybersecurity and Regulatory Challenges Digital transformation also creates new risks. Banks hold sensitive customer information and manage high-value transactions. A security failure can lead to financial loss, service disruption and damage to customer trust. Cybersecurity must therefore remain a core part of digital banking. Banks need strong access controls, secure APIs, data encryption, regular system checks and clear incident response plans. A Reuters report published on 30 October 2026 said the Reserve Bank of India was increasing cybersecurity scrutiny of lenders after a rise in attacks. The report highlighted concerns about API vulnerabilities, third-party risks and banks' readiness for AI-related threats. Financial institutions must also follow rules set by regulators in the markets where they operate. These may include requirements for customer verification, data protection, transaction reporting, record keeping and risk management. It identified investment in AI infrastructure, cloud platforms, cybersecurity, software and data technologies. Digital twin (DT) technology has become a significant advancement in smart manufacturing and is increasingly being adopted in pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industries under the concepts of industry 4.0 and pharma 4.0. A digital twin generates a synchronized virtual image of physical manufacturing system that continuously exchanges in real time information for process monitoring, prediction and optimization. This review discusses the architecture and framework of digital systems including physical components, virtual models, and data management platforms. It explains the functional architecture and interactive mapping of DT-based protection systems and highlight the role of supporting technologies such as Internet of Things (IoT), process analytical technology (PAT), cloud computing, machine learning, and manufacturing execution systems. Using digital twins in pharmaceutical production for process design, quality control, predictive maintenance, material tracking and continuous manufacturing is also presented. different modelling approaches including mechanistic, data driven, and hybrid models are discussed along with their significance in process optimization and decision making. Furthermore, the review investigates the application of digital twin technology in biopharmaceutical production as well as its ability to raise product quality and production efficiency. challenges associated with implementation such as data security commerce system integration computational requirements and regulatory compliance are also addressed. finally further development including artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (MI), edge computing, blockchain technology and cloud-based DT systems are highlighted. digital twin technology offers significant opportunities for improving pharmaceutical manufacturing efficacy reliability and product quality, making it a potentially useful tool for smart manufacturing systems of the future.

documents.abstract: Abstract Irrigation water is a recognized pathway for pre-harvest contamination of fresh produce, yet conventional laboratory testing limits monitoring frequency and timeliness of management decisions. This critical review examines how digital technologies - Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors, rapid biosensors and molecular methods, and artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning - may support irrigation water monitoring and pre-harvest food safety. Literature was purposively selected from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink and IEEE Xplore, with an initial scoping from January 2018 to October 2026; the final 29 peer-reviewed studies that met critical relevance criteria clustered between 2020 and 2026, including two 2026 early-online articles, reflecting the recent emergence of this field. The review was complemented by guidance from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Codex Alimentarius Commission (2023), World Health Organization (WHO) and United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA 2024 Final Rule on Pre-Harvest Agricultural Water). The synthesis shows that IoT systems can increase monitoring frequency for physicochemical parameters and support baseline characterization and anomaly detection, while rapid biosensors and molecular assays offer more direct detection of microbial hazards with reduced time-to-result compared with conventional culture. AI approaches can assist pattern recognition, risk prediction and interpretation of multi-parameter data. However, physicochemical measurements cannot independently confirm microbiological safety, and sensor accuracy, calibration drift, matrix interference, field validation and model transferability remain critical limitations. Integrated digital monitoring may support risk-based water management when combined with validated microbial testing and clear response procedures, but evidence that it directly reduces produce contamination under routine farming conditions remains limited. Recommendations are provided for strengthening field validation and implementation, particularly in resource-limited locations.

The growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education raises important questions about its contribution to students’ independent learning outcomes. This study examines whether structured AI-assisted learning improves university students’ independent English language proficiency compared with unrestricted AI use and conventional instruction. A quantitative, quasi-experimental design is proposed involving 150 undergraduate and postgraduate students assigned to three instructional groups. English proficiency is assessed through pre-tests, post-tests, and delayed tests conducted without AI assistance, covering grammar, vocabulary, academic writing, reading comprehension, and speaking. Regression analysis is proposed to examine the roles of instructional approach, self-regulated learning, prior AI experience, baseline proficiency, and age in explaining proficiency gains. The study seeks to distinguish AI-supported task performance from independently demonstrated language competence and retained learning. Its anticipated contribution is to inform evidence-based integration of GenAI into university language education, emphasising structured use, learner autonomy, and independent assessment.

Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) is a significant solution in software defect prediction (SDP) when historical data is unavailable. In CPDP, the defect data of another project (called the source project) is used to train the model. Different training and test projects may have different feature distributions. Divergence in data distribution between source and target projects adversely affects prediction performance, and the semantic information of the tokens cannot be captured adequately. However, most of the existing deep learning approaches assume that these two projects have a uniform distribution, so the features extracted from these deep learning models are not optimal. Moreover, these approaches neglected the information about the class to which the sample belonged and were unable to discriminate the samples according to the class information. To address this issue, we proposed a framework, TC3, that exploits the combination of contrastive and transfer learning integrated with the CNN-CodeBERT model to learn class-discriminative information and obtain more transferable features for the target project. The proposed model was evaluated on PROMISE datasets. The proposed model achieved an absolute F1-score improvement of 0.047 to 0.107, corresponding to a relative improvement of 7.89% to 19.96%, and an absolute AUC improvement of 0.014 to 0.148, corresponding to a relative improvement of 2.18% to 29.19% as compared to the baseline methods.

In the ongoing AI boom—now supercharged by large language models and generative AI tools—the rapid integration of AI into health care and public health has created an urgent need for professionals who combine deep domain expertise (clinical, epidemiological, ethical, and contextual expertise in health and public health) with AI fluency (the ability to understand, critically evaluate, use, and oversee AI systems effectively). Without domain guidance, AI risks producing biased, unsafe, or contextually irrelevant outputs that compromise patient safety and exacerbate disparities. Conversely, domain experts lacking AI fluency may underuse or misuse these technologies, missing opportunities to improve care quality, operational efficiency, and population health. A foundational understanding of the modern AI system stack—comprising energy, accelerators, infrastructure, models, and applications—empowers health professionals to make informed decisions on adoption, evaluation, governance, and ethical use without needing to code or build models themselves. This stack framework highlights critical interdependencies and health care–specific challenges, including regulatory compliance, data privacy, sustainability, and resource constraints, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This paper argues that cultivating domain-AI bilingualism is essential for safe, effective, and equitable AI integration worldwide. It outlines the 5-layer AI system stack applied to health care, key reasons for hybrid expertise, and a practical 4-step pathway: awakening (recognizing AI’s transformative role), intrepidity (courageously engaging foundational AI concepts), bilingualism (translating between clinical needs and AI capabilities), and visionary leadership (driving organizational and policy readiness). It outlines major barriers, targeted strategies, and recommendations for educators, institutions, and policymakers. By bridging domain knowledge with AI fluency, health professionals can direct—rather than be directed by—AI technologies, including emerging agentic systems, toward more precise, sustainable, and human-centered outcomes while mitigating risks. This hybrid capability represents a nonnegotiable competency for the health workforce for thriving in the post-2026 AI era.

documents.abstract: In response to practical problems in innovation and entrepreneurship education for emerging engineering in local application-oriented universities — including weak industrial alignment, limited practice scenarios, and insufficient integration of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy — this paper focuses on mechanical and electrical majors and develops a dual-wheel education framework: the endogenous drive of theoretical and practical teaching, the exogenous drive of industrial demand and skills competitions. It integrates AI technology throughout teaching, practice and evaluation, and establishes a school-enterprise-government collaborative education mechanism. In line with the development needs of Quanzhou’s intelligent manufacturing industry, teaching reforms are implemented across four dimensions: curriculum system optimisation, practice platform construction, teaching staff development and evaluation mechanism improvement. Taking mechanical and electrical majors at Quanzhou University of Information Engineering as the pilot, this study adopts an action research approach and evaluates implementation effects through questionnaire surveys, practical performance assessment and competition outcome analysis. The pilot findings suggest that this model may improve students’ engineering practical skills and innovation and entrepreneurship literacy, and offers a potential practical approach for emerging engineering education reform in local application-oriented universities.

Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) is a human-centered conceptual framework for continuously adaptive AI experiences. The framework explores how artificial intelligence might adapt not only to an individual's longer-range goals, interests, knowledge, and preferences, but also to meaningful changes that occur as an experience unfolds. The paper introduces a developing Dynamic A/B model: Dynamic A provides adaptive direction around the individual's goals and intended destination, while Dynamic B introduces state-aware responsiveness to the individual's immediate circumstances. Together, they express a central principle of the framework: A remembers the destination. B respects the human being who has to get there. Version 1.0 explores potential applications in education, experiential travel, professional environments, healthcare communication, and creative work, while emphasizing human agency, privacy, appropriate boundaries, and future research and validation.

documents.abstract: Purpose: To examine the relationship between economic sustainability, innovation, and sustainable development as key determinants of the resilience of modern economic systems and identify strategic approaches for strengthening resilience through digital transformation. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study employed a qualitative research design based on a systematic review of scientific literature, comparative analysis, and conceptual synthesis. The review covered 31 studies (2020–2026) retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, supplemented by Google Scholar, and identified the principal mechanisms that enhance the adaptability and long-term stability of economic systems. Research Limitation: The study is conceptual and based on secondary sources. Future research should validate the proposed framework using empirical evidence from different sectors. Findings: The results show that economic sustainability is closely linked to integrating technological and digital innovations into production and management processes. Structural adaptability, system integration, stakeholder participation, human capital development, and effective resource management were identified as key prerequisites for sustainable growth and resilience. Automation, digitalisation, and artificial intelligence improve business processes, increase operational efficiency, and support sustainable development by integrating economic, environmental, and social objectives. Practical Implication: The findings guide policymakers and business leaders in designing innovation-driven strategies that enhance economic resilience. Social Implication: Strengthening economic sustainability promotes long-term stability, social well-being, environmental responsibility, and resilience. Originality/Value: The study integrates the established constructs of economic sustainability, innovation, digital transformation, and resilience into one framework; what is new is the crisis-digital paradigm, which treats digital tools as a system-forming element of resilience management.

The rapid development of digital technology makes it important for young learners to become familiar with the basic concepts of artificial intelligence (AI). Many elementary school students use AI-enabled applications in their daily lives, such as voice assistants and content recommendation systems, without necessarily understanding how these technologies work. This community service activity introduced basic AI concepts to 28 Grade VI students at State Elementary School 26, Bengkulu City, on 27 August 2026, through interactive lectures, educational games, question-and-answer sessions, and simple demonstrations. Descriptive observations of student participation during the activities indicated enthusiasm and engagement with examples of AI, its benefits, and its risks. No formal evaluation instrument, pre-test/post-test scores, or numerical outcome measurements were available; therefore, the extent of learning improvement cannot be quantified. The activity provides an initial model for introducing age-appropriate AI literacy in elementary schools.

Workplace mental health challenges are prevalent in high-demand, male-dominated industries such as transportation, where job design, safety risk, and cultural norms may discourage help-seeking behaviors. However, limited evidence exists on whether workplace mental health training leads to sustained outcomes in real-world organizational settings. Leadership-focused mental health training has demonstrated improvements in stigma reduction and resilience, yet few studies examine whether these effects are sustained beyond the immediate post-training period. This evaluation examined the 6-month outcomes of The Working Mind for Managers, a manager-focused mental health training program, within a large Canadian transportation company. Data were collected between June 2022 and August 2024. Using a repeated-measures design, matched pre-training and 6-month follow-up survey data were analyzed to assess mental health stigma, resilience, confidence to address workplace mental health issues, and self-care practices. Results indicated sustained reductions in mental health stigma, with the strongest changes observed in workplace-relevant domains, including work-related beliefs/competency and perceptions of responsibility. Managers demonstrated significant improvements in resilience and confidence, along with modest increases in self-care practices. Findings are interpreted within social cognitive and adult learning frameworks, alongside organizational and implementation perspectives, highlighting the role of leadership capacity in sustaining workplace mental health training. These results contribute to the limited evidence on long-term outcomes and provide practice-relevant insights for implementing and sustaining manager-focused mental health training in real-world workplace settings.

Abstract Video-based instruction can support students’ understanding of abstract chemical concepts, but its effectiveness depends largely on the use of appropriate instructional strategies. This study examined the effects of cueing and self-explanation on chemistry video learning in terms of learning performance, intrinsic motivation, cognitive load, and visual attention. To examine whether these effects differed across chemistry learning tasks with different cognitive demands, two experiments were conducted. Experiment 1 employed a concept-knowing task, whereas Experiment 2 employed a knowledge-application task. A total of 60 grade 10 students were randomly assigned to one of the two experiments. Each experiment used a 3 (no cue, color-based cue, or contour-based cue) × 2 (with or without self-explanation) between-subjects factorial design. Fixation duration and fixation count were used to assess visual attention. Subjective workload was assessed using a self-report questionnaire, with pupil diameter providing additional evidence related to cognitive effort. The findings showed that cueing significantly affected learning performance, visual attention (fixation duration and fixation count), and pupil diameter, but no significant differences were found between the two cueing types. Self-explanation significantly improved learning performance, intrinsic motivation, and visual attention. The effects of cueing and self-explanation did not differ significantly between the two learning tasks. These findings suggest that chemistry educators can integrate cueing and self-explanation into video-based instruction to support both conceptual understanding and knowledge application.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are emerging as generalist tools capable of interpreting clinical language and supporting healthcare professionals across diverse medical contexts and tasks, making electronic health records (EHRs) a natural and powerful setting for their deployment. Yet realizing this potential safely and effectively in real-world practice requires solutions adapted to EHR users' needs and context. To propose a new paradigm for medical LLM development and evaluation that places EHR users, data, and EHR infrastructure at its center. In this narrative review, we propose three mutually reinforcing pillars of the EHR ecosystem: the daily users of these systems, such as physicians and nurses; the rich and detailed EHR data produced through routine clinical care; and the EHR system as institutional and technical infrastructure. We then examine the role these pillars play in LLM development and evaluation. We show that daily EHR users provide essential input for aligning LLMs with real clinical needs; EHR data offer the most meaningful foundation for model alignment and assessment; and the EHR system as infrastructure shapes what effective and responsible deployment looks like. Together, these pillars are shown to play an essential role in developing trustworthy and useful LLMs adapted to clinical applications, conducting reliable and meaningful evaluations, and assessing the impact of LLMs in real healthcare settings. A paradigm centered on EHR users, data, and systems is needed to develop, evaluate, and deploy LLMs that are trustworthy, useful, and adapted to real-world clinical practice.

documents.abstract: This study investigates the association between ChatGPT use for learning and Tourism English proficiency among hospitality and tourism students at Egyptian public universities, examining self-regulated learning (SRL) and intrinsic motivation (SIM) as mediating mechanisms. A quantitative cross-sectional design was adopted, with online survey data collected from 795 students across nine public universities. All participants reported using ChatGPT for English-language learning. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed to assess the measurement and structural models, including construct reliability, validity, and common method bias. The results indicate that ChatGPT use is positively associated with perceived communicative proficiency in Tourism English, SRL, and intrinsic motivation. Both SRL and SIM partially mediate the relationship between ChatGPT use and perceived communicative proficiency. These findings underscore the potential of generative AI to support autonomous learning and intrinsic motivation in Tourism English education. However, proficiency was self-reported and therefore reflects perceived rather than objectively demonstrated competence.

The diffusion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence has transformed contemporary learning ecologies, reshaping the embodied, relational, and affective configurations through which participation and belonging are constructed. Hybrid learning environments increasingly emerge as spaces where physical and digital dimensions, technological mediation, communicative practices, and affective processes interact (Floridi, 2014). Within this framework, inclusion cannot be reduced to technological access; it must be understood as the co-construction of participation by bodies, technologies, and interactions. This perspective aligns with embodied cognition approaches (Gallagher, 2005) and sociocultural perspectives that emphasize the mediational nature of learning (Vygotsky, 1978). In contexts involving students with visual impairments, accessibility and relational belonging are deeply interconnected (Pérez-Pereira & Conti-Ramsden, 1999). Emotionally aware learning environments should therefore be understood not merely as systems that detect emotional states but as relational ecologies that sustain affective attunement and shared participation (Stern, 1985). Digital assessment has become a strategic component of online higher education, supporting not only the certification of learning outcomes but also feedback processes, student monitoring and quality assurance (JISC, 2020). Recent technological developments have expanded the possibilities of assessment through Artificial Intelligence (AI), learning analytics and immersive technologies, which are increasingly associated with personalised feedback, adaptive assessment, data-informed decision making and authentic learning experiences (Holmes et al., 2023; Kamalov et al., 2023). While the educational potential of these technologies has been widely discussed, less attention has been devoted to their institutional formalisation. Technological innovation does not automatically translate into institutional adoption. Universities may experiment with innovative tools without integrating them into policies, governance structures, assessment strategies or quality assurance systems. For this reason, understanding how emerging technologies are represented within institutional documentation can provide valuable insights into the maturity of digital assessment ecosystems. Women face multiple challenges in achieving financial independence and personal safety. Although digital solutions exist, entrepreneurship guidance and emergency safety mechanisms are often provided separately. Women interested in starting businesses may lack structured information about startup opportunities, investment requirements, essential skills, financial assistance, and implementation procedures. Personal safety also remains a concern during travel, education, employment, and daily activities. This paper proposes ShaktiSafe, an integrated mobile application designed to address both challenges through a unified platform. The system consists of a Women Empowerment Module and a Women Safety Module. The empowerment module provides categorized business ideas, estimated investments, required qualifications, essential resources, and step-by-step implementation guidance. The safety module incorporates SOS alerts, voice-activated assistance, live location sharing, and emergency contact management. Artificial intelligence can support business discovery and information access, while mobile computing, database management, and location-based services enable essential functions. Multilingual interaction and an accessible interface are considered to support users with different levels of digital literacy. By integrating economic guidance with personal safety features, ShaktiSafe aims to promote awareness, entrepreneurial participation, confidence, and financial independence.

documents.abstract: This article argues that older adults’ engagement with healthcare systems supported by artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be explained solely by access to technology or individual levels of digital literacy. The central claim is that when older adults are unable to benefit fully from these systems, the problem is often framed as a personal failure to adapt, whereas the deeper issue is a form of sociotechnical exclusion produced at the intersection of data representation, design norms, limited explainability, inadequate institutional support, and age-based bias. To explore this issue, the article draws on a composite case involving an older woman who struggles to use an AI-supported chronic disease monitoring application. It first examines the opportunities associated with artificial intelligence in the care of older adults and the conceptual tensions surrounding these technologies. It then presents the composite case and analyses it through the lenses of digital exclusion, digital ageism, participatory design, care ethics, and nursing practice. The article concludes that the success of artificial intelligence in healthcare should be assessed not only in terms of accuracy, speed, and efficiency, but also in terms of its capacity to involve older adults in care processes in ways that are understandable, safe, fair, and dignified.

documents.abstract: The twenty-first century has witnessed an unprecedented convergence of language, technology, and artificial intelligence (AI), fundamentally reshaping literary production, interpretation, and dissemination. English, as the dominant language of digital communication and technological innovation, has become central to the global exchange of knowledge, creative expression, and computational systems. Simultaneously, AI technologies, particularly natural language processing and generative language models, have transformed traditional notions of authorship, creativity, and literary aesthetics. These developments have become especially significant within the framework of Metamodernism, a cultural paradigm characterized by oscillation between sincerity and irony, optimism and skepticism, reality and virtuality. The present study investigates the evolving role of the English language in the technological era and examines how AI influences the literature of the metamodern age. Employing a qualitative research methodology based on textual analysis and interdisciplinary literary criticism, the paper synthesizes insights from digital humanities, media studies, linguistic theory, and contemporary literary criticism. It argues that AI should not be viewed merely as a technological instrument but as a collaborative participant in literary production that challenges conventional definitions of creativity and textual authority. Furthermore, the study explores how English functions as the principal medium through which AI systems learn, generate, and disseminate literary texts, thereby reinforcing its global cultural influence. The findings suggest that while AI introduces ethical and aesthetic challenges, it also expands creative possibilities and redefines literary expression in the metamodern era.

Background/Objectives: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in healthcare has shown promise for analyzing complex data and identifying patterns that can enhance clinical decision-making and patient care. Patient complaints represent a valuable yet underutilized data source for improving healthcare quality and patient safety. This study aimed to investigate whether an AI-driven model could effectively categorize patient complaints to extract actionable insights that support person-centered care and nursing practice to improve care quality. Method: An explorative study design was conducted as a pilot project. A total of 368 patient complaint reports collected by a Patients’ Advisory Committee were analyzed using AI-driven clustering and classification techniques. The complaints were pre-processed through text cleaning, tokenization, and vectorization before being analyzed with various clustering algorithms. Results: The AI-based classification identified four main areas that directly or indirectly influenced patients’ perceptions of care quality: (1) Care and Treatment, (2) Communication, (3) Administrative Management, and (4) Availability. These areas encompassed themes such as diagnostic delays, poor communication, fragmented administrative processes, and limited accessibility. The results highlighted that communication failures, insufficient empathy, and lack of continuity were central to patient dissatisfaction. Automated analysis enabled the identification of recurring issues and systemic weaknesses that traditional manual review methods often overlook. Conclusion: This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility and potential of using an AI-driven model to categorize patient complaints and identify patterns that may provide actionable insights for person-centered care and nursing practice to improve quality of care. The multilabel approach enabled an efficient and systematic analysis of complex complaints and may, following further validation, offer a scalable and consistent basis for understanding patient concerns. In nursing practice, integrating AI into patient feedback systems could support the earlier identification of recurring concerns and contribute to more responsive, evidence-informed, and person-centered quality improvement. However, larger datasets, independent expert validation, and careful consideration of ethical, legal, and governance requirements are needed before the model can be implemented more broadly.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Big Data analytics are increasingly transforming vocational education by enabling personalized learning experiences and supporting data-driven educational practices. This study examines the influence of AI-powered personalized learning and Big Data analytics on student engagement, vocational skill development, learning efficiency, and overall program satisfaction at Vocational Colleges in Henan Province. A quantitative research design was adopted, and structured questionnaires were administered to 250 participants from the vocational education environment. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability and validity testing, ANOVA, and regression analysis to evaluate the proposed relationships among the study variables. The findings indicate positive participant perceptions of AI-based personalized learning, with high mean scores for AI personalization (4.215), student engagement (4.200), skill readiness (4.187), learning efficiency (4.210), and program satisfaction (4.220). Both regression and mediation analyses revealed positive associative and indirect links between AI personalization, the processing of big data, learner engagement and the vocational learning outcomes. However, ANOVA results did not show statistically significant effects of AI on skill readiness (p = 0.222), AI combined with Big Data on skill readiness (p = 0.258), AI on learning efficiency (p = 0.348), or AI on satisfaction (p = 0.348). Thus, the findings indicate positive participant perceptions and significant associative and mediating relationships, while the non-significant ANOVA results do not support direct effects of AI on several vocational learning outcomes.

Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are evolving from passive decision-support tools into autonomous digital workers capable of planning, reasoning, invoking tools, accessing enterprise resources, and executing business actions with varying degrees of autonomy. While enterprises maintain mature governance models for human identities, service accounts, and application identities, existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) frameworks do not adequately address the governance challenges introduced by autonomous agents. Unlike conventional applications, agents dynamically determine execution paths, invoke reusable skills, delegate tasks to peer agents, and perform privileged actions across enterprise systems. These characteristics define a new class of enterprise identity that requires dedicated governance, authorization, and accountability controls. This paper proposes the Enterprise Agent Identity Governance Framework (EAIGF), which treats autonomous agents as first-class enterprise identities subject to lifecycle management, quantitative trust classification, privileged access governance, and end-to-end accountability. The framework's principal constructs form an identity layer comprising the Agent Identity Registry (AIR), the Agent Provisioning Certificate, Agent Trust Tiering driven by an explicit Agent Identity Risk Score (AIRS) formula, Agent Privileged Access Management (Agent-PAM), and a Delegated Trust Chain with Agent Identity Lineage for multi-agent accountability. These constructs are enforced through a policy-mediated runtime boundary that performs capability projection and risk-adaptive authorization. A reference implementation realizing the registry, the AIRS formula, capability projection, and risk-adaptive authorization correctly enforced all ten governance scenarios in the evaluation with zero false-permits on disallowed capabilities and a mean authorization overhead of approximately 0.015 ms per request. A larger randomized evaluation over 600 authorization requests across 80 agents and 25 reusable skills reproduced this result and, against a naive whole-skill authorization baseline, reduced the exposed capability surface by 66.7 percent while blocking every attempted privilege escalation through delegation. A synthetic financial-services walkthrough demonstrates how Identity Governance and Administration (IGA), Privileged Access Management (PAM), and Zero Trust principles extend to agentic environments. EAIGF provides a practical blueprint for governing autonomous agents at scale while preserving least privilege, accountability, and operational resilience.

The emergence of artificial intelligence in the field of cultural heritage has sparked debates that often oscillate between enthusiasm and apprehension. However, AI is no longer a future possibility but a present reality, already integrated into numerous processes of research, communication, and access to knowledge. From this perspective, the real challenge is not whether we should accept or reject AI, but rather how to incorporate it in a responsible, critical, and meaningful way that serves the objectives of heritage management. The most significant contribution of AI to cultural heritage does not lie primarily in the automation of tasks, but in its ability to expand and enrich the contexts through which heritage is understood, making specialized knowledge accessible to increasingly diverse audiences. Heritage research produces a vast amount of rigorous information that often remains confined to academic or professional environments. In this regard, artificial intelligence can help translate, connect, and disseminate such knowledge without compromising scientific rigor. From the perspective of heritage education, this capacity is particularly important, as the preservation of heritage largely depends on citizens’ ability to know, understand, and value it. Conservation is not achieved solely through legal protection measures or technical interventions; it also requires social awareness and public engagement. By facilitating access to knowledge and promoting new forms of interaction with cultural assets, AI can contribute to strengthening the relationship between communities and their heritage. Nevertheless, AI should always be understood as a tool rather than an end in itself. Critical judgment, interpretation, and scientific responsibility remain inherently human competencies that cannot be delegated to technology. Consequently, the greatest potential of artificial intelligence lies in helping heritage knowledge move beyond specialized circles and become a genuine public good, fostering a more informed, engaged, and culturally aware society.

Elementary teachers in rural Indonesia face substantial barriers in delivering the entrepreneurship theme of the Projek Penguatan Profil Pelajar Pancasila (P5) [Project for Strengthening the Pancasila Learner Profile], the national program that grounds character education in Indonesia’s five founding principles, particularly in designing authentic assessment and in integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into project-based instruction. This study developed and validated an AI assessment model to strengthen teachers’ pedagogical, professional, social, and personal competencies. A five-stage Research and Development design comprised needs analysis, model design, expert validation, and staged field trials with a purposive sample of 19 teachers, followed by dissemination to all 91 teachers across the 12 schools of Gomo District, South Nias Regency. Only four teachers (21%) had received prior digital training. Expert validation confirmed feasibility across four domains (75.50–90.83%), and staged trials improved to an overall mean of 4.09. Pre-post comparisons showed gains in all four competency domains (+0.75 to +1.16), alongside a 63% rise in forum engagement and 96% platform uptime. Dissemination produced consistently positive reception across six constructs (overall M = 4.49, SD = 0.19), with perceived usefulness and behavioral intention rated most favorably. Embedding adaptive AI assessment within contextually grounded content can strengthen teacher professionalism in under-resourced rural schools.

This paper examines why historical and current protections have not consistently provided early recognition, diagnosis, treatment, return to service, or whole-of-life care for military and emergency services personnel affected by service-related psychological and physical harm. It applies Dmitry Nikolaenko’s three regimes of scientific recognition—Accompanying Science, Warning Science, and Critical Reconstruction—to New Zealand Defence Force and emergency services contexts. The analysis considers psychological trauma, moral injury, cumulative occupational stress, cancers, and other chronic conditions associated with repeated exposure to toxins, toxic environments, and temperature-related stressors. Evidence is drawn from New Zealand legislation, operational arrangements, official reports, published research, compensation processes, and existing health data systems. The paper argues that Nikolaenko’s model remains applicable when attention shifts from environmental contamination to human health, but that Critical Reconstruction does not by itself specify what must happen after institutional non-recognition has been identified. Two further regimes are therefore proposed. Critical Practice addresses immediate protection, monitoring, data preservation, redress, and operational change. Critical Regeneration redesigns the relationship between scientific inquiry, governance responsibility, law, occupational health, and operational practice so that future harm is recognized and acted on earlier. Together, the five regimes form the Nikolaenko-Alexander Model.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Ergonomic challenges within university learning environments are increasingly recognized as important determinants of student health and academic performance.However, most studies in low-and middle-income countries focus on quantitative assessments, with limited attention to students' lived experiences.This study employed a qualitative descriptive design using open-ended responses collected via an online survey administered to 352 undergraduate students at the University of Calabar, Nigeria.Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis to explore students' experiences, perceived impacts, and coping mechanisms related to ergonomic challenges in their learning environments.Three major themes emerged: (1) Physical strain and bodily discomfort, characterized by musculoskeletal pain and visual strain due to non-adjustable furniture and poor environmental conditions; (2) Cognitive exhaustion and academic disruption, where discomfort impaired concentration, reduced engagement, and contributed to absenteeism; and (3) Institutional neglect and adaptive coping, highlighting the absence of supportive infrastructure and students' reliance on improvised strategies.These findings demonstrate that poor ergonomic conditions extend beyond physical discomfort to significantly affect mental well-being and academic outcomes.Ergonomic deficiencies in university settings represent a critical but underaddressed public health issue.Interventions should prioritize human-centered classroom design, inclusive infrastructure, and institutional policies that support student well-being.

Generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities to strengthen self-directed learning in nursing education when its integration is supported by a structured pedagogical design. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the E-PAGIA strategy, organized into planning, construction, self-monitoring, and interaction/transfer stages, on self-directed learning among nursing students. A quantitative, quasi-experimental, longitudinal study was conducted with 128 students, distributed between an experimental group and a control group, with 64 participants in each. The intervention lasted eight weeks. Self-directed learning was assessed using the Self-Directed Learning Instrument, considering both the overall score and its dimensions. The groups showed comparable baseline scores. Following the intervention, the experimental group increased its mean overall score from 65.00 to 82.35 points, whereas the control group increased from 65.75 to 69.46. Improvements in the experimental group were observed across all four dimensions and were particularly pronounced in learning motivation and planning and implementation. Analysis adjusted for baseline scores confirmed significant differences between groups and showed a large effect associated with the strategy. The findings indicate that E-PAGIA can foster self-directed learning when generative artificial intelligence is integrated as cognitive support within a pedagogical sequence that preserves students' intellectual responsibility, teacher mediation, and critical verification of information. The study concludes that E-PAGIA represents a relevant pedagogical innovation for nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This review covers human–artificial intelligence collaboration in making decisions, observing how scholarship has moved from thinking of AI as a passive tool to considering it as an active actor in healthcare, management, and ethics. While AI systems provide for efficient data processing and pattern recognition, humans provide contextual understanding, ethical judgment, creativity, and accountability. Previous literature suggests that well-designed collaboration between humans and AI may outperform completely automated decision-making. However, several key challenges persist, like bias, lack of transparency, miscalibrated trust, poorly defined distribution of roles, and accountability gaps. To handle these concerns, human-centered design, explainability in AI, well-articulated guidelines on ethical consideration, and mechanisms that effectively introduce oversight remain at the core of literature. These approaches jointly try to ensure that human–AI decision-making systems are fair, accountable, and trustworthy in high-stakes and critical settings
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study aims to evaluate ANSIA (SIDIA Assistant), an artificial intelligence -based chatbot program at Universitas Negeri Surabaya, using the CIPP (Context, Input, Process, Product) evaluation model. A descriptive-evaluative qualitative approach was employed. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and document analysis involving developers from the Directorate of Digital Learning Innovation (DIPD) at UNESA as key informants, as well as six lecturers and 19 students from the Office Administration Education undergraduate study program, cohorts 2024 and 2025, as primary informants. Data credibility was examined through source triangulation, and the data were analyzed using the Miles and Huberman interactive model. The evaluation revealed four major gaps. In the context component, ANSIA was developed without a formal needs assessment, resulting in a gap in user awareness. In the input component, server infrastructure and WhatsApp integration were not adequately supported by a dedicated budget, formal socialization, or sufficient operational guidelines. In the process component, an increase in aggregate server-log access did not fully reflect student use of ANSIA at the study-program level. Interview findings indicated that preferences for commercial artificial intelligence tools and limitations in the internal knowledge base were factors associated with low utilization. In the product component, a discrepancy emerged between developers’ claims of 24-hour service availability and users’ experiences in accessing and using the system. The study recommends expanding the scientific knowledge base, providing visual user guides, allocating a dedicated budget, and integrating ANSIA into teaching and learning activities. ABSTRAK Penelitian ini bertujuan mengevaluasi program chatbot berbasis artificial intelligence, yaitu ANSIA (Asisten SIDIA), di Universitas Negeri Surabaya menggunakan model evaluasi CIPP (Context, Input, Process, Product). Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan desain deskriptif evaluatif. Data dikumpulkan melalui wawancara mendalam dan dokumentasi yang melibatkan pengembang dari Direktorat Inovasi Pembelajaran Digital (DIPD) UNESA sebagai informan kunci serta enam dosen dan 19 mahasiswa Program Studi S1 Pendidikan Administrasi Perkantoran angkatan 2024 dan 2025 sebagai informan utama. Keabsahan data diperiksa melalui triangulasi sumber, sedangkan analisis data menggunakan model interaktif Miles dan Huberman. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan empat kesenjangan utama. Pada komponen context, pengembangan ANSIA tidak didahului asesmen kebutuhan formal sehingga ditemukan kesenjangan kesadaran (awareness gap) pengguna. Pada komponen input, dukungan infrastruktur server dan integrasi WhatsApp belum diimbangi anggaran khusus, sosialisasi formal, serta panduan operasional yang memadai. Pada komponen process, peningkatan jumlah akses berdasarkan log server agregat tidak sepenuhnya mencerminkan pemanfaatan ANSIA oleh mahasiswa di tingkat program studi. Temuan wawancara menunjukkan bahwa kecenderungan menggunakan artificial intelligence komersial dan keterbatasan basis pengetahuan internal menjadi faktor yang berkaitan dengan rendahnya pemanfaatan tersebut. Pada komponen product, terdapat perbedaan antara klaim pengembang mengenai ketersediaan layanan selama 24 jam dan pengalaman pengguna dalam mengakses serta memanfaatkan sistem. Penelitian ini merekomendasikan perluasan basis pengetahuan ilmiah, penyediaan panduan visual, pengalokasian anggaran khusus, dan integrasi ANSIA dalam kegiatan pembelajaran.

Corporate governance is one of the areas most affected by the economic, technological and social transformations that have taken place in recent years. The emergence of complex digital ecosystems, the automation of decision-making processes and the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) are redefining not only the way organisations operate (Abriani, 2020), but also the epistemological and value-based assumptions on which strategic decisions are founded. Modern business is undergoing a profound transformation (Rossi, 2012). Corporate governance, traditionally understood as a set of rules, structures and mechanisms designed to ensure the control and management of the enterprise, now tends to take on a dynamic and relational form, in which human actors, technologies, information networks and socio-cultural contexts interact (Fenwick et al., 2018). At the same time, the issue of inclusion and organisational well-being has taken on increasing importance: organisations are increasingly called upon to respond not only to economic performance targets, but also to demands for equity, social sustainability and the valuing of differences (Schneider, 2022). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 65-67. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Generative AI and New Narratives of the Self.

Mental-health strain has become a routine feature of organizational life, yet managers and organizations continue to struggle to explain why capable employees make avoidable errors, why teams lose coordination under pressure, and why judgment quality deteriorates during periods of sustained stress. This article argues that executive function decay—the temporary or chronic degradation of working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility—is a central but underrecognized mechanism linking mental strain to workplace performance failures.Drawing on research from cognitive neuroscience, clinical psychology, and organizational behavior, I explain how common forms of mental-health morbidity and burnout impair the cognitive capacities that support judgment, emotional regulation, and adaptive decision-making. I show how executive function decay produces predictable patterns of managerial behavior, team dysfunction, and organizational drift that are misattributed to motivation, attitude, or character.The article introduces a multilevel framework connecting executive function impairment to outcomes at the individual, team, and organizational levels. I then translate this framework into practical implications for leaders and HR systems, highlighting how job design, leadership behavior, workload architecture, and organizational norms can either stabilize or erode cognitive capacity. By reframing mental health as a decision-quality and organizational design issue, this article offers managers and scholars a practical lens for improving judgment, coordination, and resilience under pressure.

Motorcycles are the main mode of transportation that requires maintenance due to damage. Unfortunately, damage detection on motorcycles remains traditional, despite the potential for expert systems and artificial intelligence (AI) to facilitate more straightforward diagnosis for both motorcycle users and mechanics. That is why this research aims to develop a system with an expert system approach to diagnose damage to a motorcycle. This research applies the certainty factor (CF) expert system approach and the case-based reasoning (CBR) AI method. The study found that the expert system using the CBR method outperforms the CF method in diagnosing motorcycle damage. The CF expert system method achieves an accuracy performance of 98%. In comparison, the CBR expert system method achieves an accuracy of up to 100%, or can be equated with human mechanics in diagnosing motorcycle damage. The finding implies that CBR can effectively replace human experts in detecting motorcycle damage.

Artificial intelligence and learning analytics can identify patterns of learning risk earlier and support more differentiated allocation of formative support in higher education. Yet predictive accuracy does not by itself make an educational decision valid: evidence must be interpretable in relation to learning goals, explanations must not be confused with causal diagnosis, and final support decisions should remain subject to professional review and learner participation. This article develops a human-supervised decision architecture and computationally illustrates its predictive and support-allocation components through a reproducible simulation of 10,000 synthetic learner-course observations without using personal data. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were compared under class imbalance. Decision thresholds were selected on a validation subset by minimizing a weighted decision-cost function in which missing an at-risk learner was assigned greater weight than generating an additional support-review action. On the independent test set, XGBoost achieved ROC-AUC = 0.910, PR-AUC = 0.764, recall = 0.902, F1 = 0.612, and Matthews correlation coefficient = 0.526 at a threshold of 0.220. Mean absolute SHAP values indicated that formative assessment score, task completion, attendance, prior achievement, self-regulation, engagement, learning progress, and study consistency contributed most strongly to predictions. Under the stated scenario assumptions, the AI-assisted allocation strategy produced an illustrative weighted decision cost that was 62.4% lower than a reactive end-of-term strategy and 26.9% fewer review/support actions than a simple rule-based strategy. The scenario models alert allocation and review workload only; it does not model teacher acceptance, intervention implementation, learner response, or learning effects. The methodological contribution is the integration of cost-sensitive thresholding, a mandatory teacher decision gate, SHAP-informed pedagogical reason codes, learner challenge and data correction, and workload-aware threshold governance within one auditable formative-assessment architecture. The reported metrics therefore illustrate the predictive and allocation logic of the architecture rather than the effectiveness of the pedagogical system as a whole.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Modern law enforcement agencies face the dual challenge of managing complex public safety threats while maintaining strict institutional accountability. This paper explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and advanced digital tools within modern policing frameworks. By analyzing current implementations—including predictive policing algorithms, automated facial recognition, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and AI-driven evidence management systems—this study assesses how these technologies enhance operational efficiency, accelerate response times, and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical systemic challenges, specifically targeting algorithmic bias, citizen privacy concerns, data security vulnerabilities, and the regulatory frameworks required to govern automated decision-making. Ultimately, this research provides a balanced framework for law enforcement executives and policymakers, demonstrating how agencies can leverage cutting-edge technical innovation while upholding the core principles of ethical, transparent, and community-oriented justice

Abstract Judicial artificial intelligence requires grounds for warranted reliance rather than confidence alone. This study examines how respondents in Bangladesh distinguish understandable reasons, independent validation and opportunities to challenge AI-supported recommendations. A cross-sectional analysis of 385 adult, AI-aware respondents uses seven questionnaire items without treating their mixed normative and conditional wording as a validated explainability-trust scale. The analysis combines paired endorsement comparisons, proportional-odds models with robust covariance, multiplicity adjustment and paired-outcome coefficient comparisons. Independent-validation-contingent trust was endorsed by 247 respondents (64.2%), compared with 215 (55.8%) for explanation-contingent trust: a paired difference of 8.3 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 1.6–15.1; Holm-adjusted p = .021). Access to review or appeal received greater endorsement than the ability to question recommendations (85.2% versus 65.2%; difference 20.0 points, 95% interval 14.3–25.7). None of the eight focal associations between four governance expectations and the two trust propositions remained distinguishable from zero after Holm adjustment. The joint test of differences between the four outcome-specific coefficients was also inconclusive (p = .236). These findings identify a descriptive separation between explanations, validation and remedies while providing limited adjusted evidence about how those expectations align within respondents. The predominantly student sample does not establish judicial practice, actual reliance or causal effects of explanations. The article develops a layered account of judicial AI governance that connects understandable reasons with independent evaluation and effective review, and specifies a measurement and experimental agenda for testing calibrated reliance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) may help students who are hard of hearing review spoken explanations, but transcription errors could affect access to course content. This preliminary study examined ASR errors in three Korean EBS lectures (language, mathematics, and chemistry) and an English Technology, Entertainment, Design (TED) talk. Each lecture was played on an iPad in a quiet room and transcribed using Clova Note (Naver Corporation, Seongnam, Korea) and Plaud (Plaud Inc., San Francisco, CA, USA). The outputs were compared with reference transcripts using word error rate (WER) and character error rate (CER). For Korean, WER was calculated using space-delimited eojeols; for English, it was calculated using words. In the Korean language lecture, WERs were 20.27% for Clova Note (Naver Corporation) and 13.85% for Plaud (Plaud Inc.); in mathematics, 42.78% and 54.33%; and in chemistry, 28.62% and 28.44%, respectively. In the TED talk, WERs were 3.88% and 3.10%. In mathematics, the ranking of the two tools differed between WER and CER. Error rates varied across materials and measures, but these data cannot establish comparative performance across languages or benefits for students. Future studies should examine errors in key course content and evaluate how students use verified transcripts to understand lectures.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving the teaching and learning process globally. Therefore, this study determined exploring the power of artificial intelligence (AI) for improving the teaching of business education courses in government tertiary institutions in Rivers State. Two research questions guided the study and two null hypotheses were tested. Descriptive survey research design was adopted. From a population of 99 lecturers, a census survey sampling was employed. A four-point response options questionnaire was used for data collection, and it was validated by three experts. The reliability of the instrument was established using Cronbach’s alpha which yielded coefficients of 0.79 and 0.78. Mean and Standard Deviation were used to answer the two research questions and measure the spread in respondents` opinions, while oneway analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to test the two null hypotheses at 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that all the types of AI listed were highly needed to be explored, and were very highly powerful for improving the teaching of business education courses. From the findings, it was concluded that if AI is included in the teaching of business education courses, it will transform the programme positively, lead to AI skills development and enable the learners to acquire the needed AI employability skills for the global workplace. Therefore, among other things, it was recommended that AI should be included in the business education curriculum through yearly internal curriculum review by lecturers in collaboration with their institutions and a five-year national review by all levels of government.

This study examined the feasibility of an artificial intelligence system using webcam eye tracking to estimate sustained attention performance. In a controlled laboratory study, 129 participants (mean age: 25.98 ± 2.07 years; 83.7% female) completed the AX Continuous Performance Task. Performance was operationalized as a reciprocal-log index of correct-response reaction time, with higher values indicating faster responses. Six visual scanning features were captured, and five composite models were compared: one literature-based and four derived from experimental data. All showed significant in-sample associations with performance. The weighted composite incorporating all six features provided the best in-sample fit, but participant-level split-half cross-validation yielded a modest out-of-sample association (r = 0.19). Univariate analyses linked better performance to faster jumps and lower length and speed irregularity. These findings provide preliminary evidence for webcam-derived gaze features in cognitive assessment under laboratory conditions, with further validation needed before integration into human–computer interaction applications.

Mental-health services face prolonged waiting periods, workforce pressures, and constrained inpatient capacity. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support access and continuity, but therapeutic relationships, patient safety, and accountability cannot be delegated to technology. We examined where AI-assisted mental-health support may be appropriate and what safeguards responsible adoption requires.
