documents.abstract: Occupational Safety and Health Management System (SMK3) is essential to protect hospital workers and support safe and quality healthcare services. However, its implementation may vary according to organizational and operational conditions, while evidence regarding the factors associated with SMK3 implementation at the regional hospital level remains limited. This study aimed to analyze the factors associated with SMK3 implementation at Tuan Besar Syarif Idrus Regional General Hospital, Kubu Raya Regency, West Kalimantan. An analytical quantitative study with a cross-sectional design was conducted among 180 employees. From a total workforce of 210 employees, 30 non-healthcare employees were allocated for instrument validity and reliability testing. A total of 140 respondents were selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using Spearman rank correlation and multiple linear regression with a significance level of 0.05. The results showed significant positive associations between SMK3 implementation and OHS policy (r = 0.408), management commitment (r = 0.505), human resource competence (r = 0.377), facilities and infrastructure (r = 0.659), and work environment (r = 0.306), with all p < 0.001. The multivariable regression model was significant (F = 34.721; p < 0.001) and explained 56.4% of the variance in SMK3 implementation (R² = 0.564). Facilities and infrastructure were the only significant independent predictor (β = 0.562; p < 0.001). These findings indicate that strengthening the availability, adequacy, accessibility, and maintenance of safety facilities and infrastructure should be prioritized to improve SMK3 implementation, supported by effective policies, management commitment, competent human resources, and a safe work environment.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: As AI system for detection has migrated from purely experimental demonstrations to an integral part of police, welfare, healthcare, and immigration systems, so has the lack of visibility for individuals being classified by those systems regarding how the systems work (and therefore how they can contest or correct the results produced by the systems). This chapter considers the problems of fairness and bias and explainability within detection AI using multiple in-depth case studies from the United States, the Netherlands, and India as examples of these issues as viewed through alternative ethical values derived from Sub-Saharan Africa, Indigenous and Confucian ethics. This chapter provides an argument supported by empirical research, general court documents, and regulations published between 2017 and 2025 that fair detection AI is a characteristic of a complete sociotechnical system rather than just the algorithmic part of the system. This chapter develops the concepts of the proxy problem and the opacity problem and shows how both recur across jurisdictions and decision domains. This chapter proposes a principle of contextual transparency, under which the explanation a detection system produces must serve the actual epistemic needs of the people affected by the system, in the contexts where the system’s outputs matter.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Nurses’ work productivity is a strategic indicator of hospital service quality, as nurses are directly involved in patient care, documentation, interprofessional communication, and continuous patient safety efforts. This study aimed to examine the factors associated with nurses’ work productivity in hospitals. This study employed a systematic literature review method guided by the PRISMA 2020 statement and the PECO framework. The literature search was conducted through Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and PubMed for primary studies published in Indonesian or English between 2021 and 2026. A total of 20 articles were included in the qualitative synthesis. The reviewed studies indicated that workload, occupational stress, fatigue, motivation, discipline, income, work environment, shift system, management support, and individual characteristics were associated with nurses’ productivity. Workload emerged as the most consistently reported factor, while age and educational background tended to influence productivity through physical capacity, experience, professional competence, and maturity in decision-making. Improving nurses’ productivity requires integrated hospital occupational health and safety management through workload control, improvement of the physical work environment, fatigue prevention, fair task distribution, and competency development. Keywords: Nurse Productivity, Workload, Physical Work Environment, Age, Education. ABSTRAK Produktivitas kerja perawat merupakan indikator strategis mutu pelayanan rumah sakit karena perawat berperan langsung dalam asuhan pasien, dokumentasi, komunikasi antarprofesi, dan keselamatan pasien secara berkelanjutan. Tujuan penelitian ini adalah untuk mengkaji faktor yang berhubungan dengan produktivitas kerja perawat di rumah sakit. Metode penelitian menggunakan systematic literature review dengan acuan PRISMA 2020 dan kerangka PECO. Penelusuran literatur dilakukan melalui Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, dan PubMed terhadap studi primer berbahasa Indonesia atau Inggris yang terbit pada tahun 2021-2026. Sebanyak 20 artikel diinklusi dalam sintesis kualitatif. Studi yang direview menunjukkan bahwa beban kerja, stres kerja, kelelahan, motivasi, disiplin, penghasilan, lingkungan kerja, sistem shift, dukungan manajemen, dan karakteristik individu berhubungan dengan produktivitas perawat. Beban kerja menjadi faktor yang paling konsisten, sedangkan usia dan pendidikan cenderung mempengaruhi produktivitas melalui kapasitas fisik, pengalaman, kompetensi profesional, dan kematangan pengambilan keputusan. Peningkatan produktivitas perawat memerlukan pengelolaan K3RS secara terpadu melalui pengendalian beban kerja, perbaikan lingkungan kerja fisik, pencegahan kelelahan, pembagian tugas yang adil, dan pengembangan kompetensi. Kata Kunci: Produktivitas Kerja Perawat, Beban Kerja, Lingkungan Kerja Fisik, Usia, Pendidikan.

With the pervasive integration of generative artificial intelligence across diverse social domains, user acceptance intention manifests a distinctive coexistence of "fun and fear." Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, this investigation develops an expanded model by integrating perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, and privacy concerns, whilst assessing the moderating influence of professional background. Based on 486 valid questionnaires and structural equation modeling, the model shows acceptable fit (/df = 1.88, RMSEA = 0.043, CFI/TLI > 0.90). Perceived enjoyment strengthens attitude (β = 0.324, p < 0.001) and perceived usefulness (β = 0.284, p < 0.001), while AI anxiety reduces perceived usefulness (β = -0.296, p < 0.001) and privacy concern weakens attitude (β = -0.148, p = 0.021); the core TAM path is supported (ATT BI: β = 0.643, p < 0.001; BI USE: β = 0.535, p < 0.001). By contrast, H7, H8, and H10 are not supported (p > 0.05), and professional background shows negligible moderation. These results suggest that promoting generative AI requires enhancing enjoyable interaction while reducing anxiety and privacy risks.

Artificial intelligence is used to describe, organise and interpret cultural heritage collections, yet discussion often focuses on what systems can produce rather than on the knowledge embodied in their data. This contribution approaches that problem through underwater archaeology, where the material traces of a shipwreck are encountered through historical documents, nautical charts, acoustic surveys, photographs, oral testimony and family memories. The identification of the Brazilian auxiliary ship Vital de Oliveira, torpedoed in 1944, offers a case for examining how evidence converge without becoming interchangeable. Historical records, bathymetric products and personal accounts arise from distinct processes and support different kinds of claims. Their integration therefore cannot be reduced to technical interoperability or persuasive reconstruction. Drawing on debates in digital archaeology, archival studies and the ethics of artificial intelligence, we argue that responsible heritage applications require attention to four interrelated conditions: provenance, uncertainty, interpretive plurality and responsibility. Provenance and paradata make the circumstances of data production traceable; uncertainty distinguishes observation from inference; plurality keeps divergent interpretations open to scrutiny; and responsibility addresses consent, rights, institutional decisions and the sensitivities surrounding human memory. These principles are proposed as a curatorial orientation, not as an implemented computational ontology or an assessment of an operational AI system. Although grounded in underwater cultural heritage, the argument extends to museums, libraries, archives and digital collections. The central challenge is not simply to make heritage legible to artificial intelligence, but to ensure that the limits, omissions and mediations of its evidentiary foundations remain legible to people as well.

Artificial intelligence (AI) promises greater efficiency and accessibility in online medical consultation (OMC). However, user acceptance, particularly among older adults, remains low. This paradox is not fully explained by cognitive-centric models like the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). This study investigates uniqueness neglect as a critical psychological barrier induced by standardized algorithmic interactions. Two between-subjects experiments manipulated consultation type (AI vs. human doctor) to induce differential perception of uniqueness neglect. Results revealed that AI-doctor consultation triggered stronger uniqueness neglect, which reduced acceptance through serial mediators of perceived usefulness and emotional response. The study also provides evidence that activating higher perceived usefulness is an effective intervention. Theoretically, our findings reveal a cognitive-affective serial mechanism extending beyond utilitarian model(s) of resistance to AI services. Practically, OMC platforms should design AI interactions that proactively affirm functional value to compensate for standardized procedure.

Abstract Background The rapid integration of generative AI (GenAI) into nursing education has prompted widespread concern about academic integrity and assessment validity. However, this dominant discourse may obscure a more fundamental challenge: preparing nursing students for clinical practice environments where AI already mediates triage, diagnostics, documentation, and clinical decision-making. Objective This integrative review examines how GenAI is conceptualized within the nursing education literature and investigates the extent to which current discourse addresses professional formation rather than academic compliance. Methods Following Whittemore and Knafl’s integrative review methodology, a systematic search of PubMed, Google Scholar, and SciSpace (Typeset) was conducted for literature published between January 2022 and February 2026. Two reviewers independently screened 456 records, with 119 papers meeting the inclusion criteria. The methodological quality of empirical studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Corpus-level descriptive mapping quantified dominant themes and conceptual patterns, while an interpretive synthesis examined how GenAI was framed and the extent to which professional formation elements, including identity, moral agency, and clinical judgment, were addressed. Results Of the 119 unique studies analyzed, 84% (n=100) predominantly framed GenAI as a content-generation tool and academic integrity threat. Only 35.3% (n=42) conceptualized AI as a pedagogical tool, and a critical gap was identified in professional formation: identity formation was addressed in only 10% (n=12) of papers and moral agency in just 5% (n=6). Explicit acknowledgment that AI already routinely mediates frontline clinical decisions (eg, sepsis alerts and fall risk algorithms) in current practice settings was notably absent. The discourse emphasizes governance and faculty literacy, but sustained curricula addressing nurse identity in AI-mediated care remain underdeveloped. Conclusions Current nursing education discourse predominantly frames AI as a writing tool and an academic integrity concern, failing to prepare students for the algorithmic practice environments they will inhabit. Nursing education must reframe AI as a professional formation issue, explicitly addressing how algorithms reshape clinical judgment, moral agency, and professional identity.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) is reshaping human resource (HR) management, requiring HR managers to integrate traditional HR expertise with AI-specific competencies. Despite growing research on AI-enabled human resource management, few studies have identified the competencies required by hybrid HR–Gen AI managers, particularly in emerging-market contexts. This study aims to identify and analyze these competencies in the Tunisian context and to develop an empirically grounded competency framework for AI-enabled HR transformation. Under an interpretivist paradigm and an inductive, qualitative approach, 12 semistructured interviews were conducted with hybrid HR–Gen AI managers. Using the MAXQDA tool, thematic analysis identified 49 competency codes grouped into seven competency categories: strategic, change management, human and interpersonal, technological and technical, analytic, ethical, and basic competencies. Seven individual competencies were mentioned by more than 50% of respondents, while “Gen AI-driven HR task automation” and “data privacy and confidentiality management” were identified as the most frequently cited, with each identified by 10 of the 12 participants. The findings also point to the relevance of ethical awareness, critical thinking, and a human-centered mindset in managing Gen AI-enabled HR transformation. The proposed competency framework can inform HR workforce development and organizational strategies for the responsible and effective integration of Gen AI into HR practices.

Researchers commonly manipulate chatbot anthropomorphism through social cues, whose effects vary and may introduce unintended perceptual differences. Generative AI enables an alternative: manipulating perceived characteristics through natural-language prompting. Two online experiments (N = 84 each) evaluated behavior-prescriptive and perception-goal prompting for manipulating anthropomorphism. Study 1 found no significant differences in anthropomorphism. Study 2 found significant differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism (ds = .86–.95), without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence. These findings provide initial empirical support for perception-goal prompting and suggest broader methodological possibilities for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics in human–AI communication research.

Child interviewing in sensitive judicial procedures requires environments and systems that accommodate communication (COM), ergonomic (ERG), sensory/environmental (SEN), safety/privacy (SPR), and functional needs. However, child-sensitive recommendations are not always formulated as engineering specifications directly applicable to product and system development. This study proposes the Adaptive Child Interviewing System Framework (ACISF), a structured approach for translating multidisciplinary evidence into engineering requirements for adaptive child-centred interviewing systems. Child needs (CNs) are systematically translated into functional requirements (FRs), design requirements (DRs), and engineering parameters (EPs), with the resulting relationships consolidated within a Child Need–Engineering Requirement Matrix (CNERM). Adaptability is structured through common (C), age-adaptive (AA), and individually configurable (IC) requirements. The 6–10- and 10–14-year groups provide initial configuration bands, while individual configurability accommodates variation beyond age alone. The framework integrates requirements across five design domains and is demonstrated through the conceptual development of an adaptive child-interviewing cabin addressing spatial, anthropometric, accessibility, environmental, privacy, and safety considerations. The ACISF provides a traceable requirements-engineering architecture connecting child-centred evidence with implementable design solutions and supporting subsequent technical specification, prototype development, expert assessment, usability evaluation, and empirical validation.

This study maps the development of research on educational data governance and student privacy between 2015 and 2025. It follows the structure of a bibliometric trend review and uses a Scopus-derived record set of 313 articles to analyze the analytical workflow, including annual output, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution, policy turning points, and research collaboration. The study is guided by three questions: how the volume of research changed, how the dominant vocabulary moved from learning analytics and ownership to compliance and responsible artificial intelligence, and which problems remained unresolved across the period. The results show five connected phases. From 2015 to 2017, research was organized around learning analytics, educational data mining, student tracking, data ownership, and informed consent. After the General Data Protection Regulation became applicable on May 25, 2018, the literature moved toward data protection, compliance, governance frameworks, and institutional responsibility. The COVID-19 period increased attention to remote learning privacy, online proctoring, surveillance, and vendor data sharing. From late 2022, generative artificial intelligence, ChatGPT, algorithmic bias, ethical artificial intelligence, and artificial intelligence literacy became central. The 2024-2025 frontier connected responsible artificial intelligence with high-risk education systems, human oversight, auditability, and data minimization in large language models. The study argues that compliance is necessary but insufficient. A mature governance model must connect legal duties, institutional processes, technical controls, and educational judgment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The widespread diffusion of digital technologies has transformed educational contexts, reshaping how students communicate, learn, and build social relationships. While digital platforms and social networks offer important opportunities for participation and access to knowledge, they have also contributed to new forms of relational vulnerability. Within this scenario, bullying and cyberbullying represent major educational challenges, negatively affecting psychological well-being, academic achievement, and school life. Cyberbullying differs from traditional bullying because it transcends the temporal and spatial boundaries of school, amplifying the impact of aggression through online dissemination. These phenomena are often associated with limited socio-emotional competencies, including empathy, emotional self-regulation, and conflict management. At the same time, artificial intelligence, social robotics, and emotionally aware technologies are redefining the relationship between education, learning, and social interaction. Although these tools may foster empathy and relational awareness, they also raise ethical concerns regarding emotional simulation, privacy, and the authenticity of human relationships. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 148-149. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.

Abstract Artificial intelligence intensifies children's dual position in digital environments. A child may be impersonated, groomed, profiled, extorted or depicted in synthetic sexual content; the same child may experiment with generative systems, automated deception or unauthorised-access tools and thereby become a child in conflict with law. This paper asks whether Indian law protects the first child without adultifying the second. Doctrinal analysis shows a substantial but fragmented framework. POCSO and Section 67B of the Information Technology Act address child sexual exploitation material, while the 2024 Supreme Court decision in Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish adopts a purpose-sensitive approach to possession, viewing and reporting. Yet entirely synthetic depictions that do not involve an identifiable or actual child raise unresolved questions of statutory language and harm. The 2026 amendments to the Intermediary Rules now regulate synthetically generated information through user declarations, labelling and due diligence, but do not independently define every deepfake as a crime. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act's child-specific Section 9 and the corresponding final 2025 Rules were enacted but, under the notified phased commencement, were not yet operational on 19 August 2026. For children accused of AI-assisted conduct, the Juvenile Justice Act remains adequate in principle because it demands individualised, rehabilitative inquiry; technical ability is evidence, not a proxy for maturity or mens rea. The paper recommends a child-specific, risk-based AI framework joining safety-by-design, precise synthetic-CSAM coverage, data minimisation, platform duties, evidence standards, diversion and specialised rehabilitation.

The May 2024 super geomagnetic storm provided a rare opportunity to investigate the full-chain impact of extreme space weather on the thermosphere and Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites. This study presents, for the first time, an end-to-end quantitative analysis that links high-latitude energy input, thermospheric density response, multi-model performance evaluation, and satellite orbital decay. High-latitude Joule heating increased from ~2 mW/m2 during the quiet period to 112 mW/m2 during the main phase. The hemispherically integrated heating peaked at 1822 GW, and the enhanced heating persisted for approximately 18–20 h. Swarm-A observations show that the orbital-mean neutral density at ~470 km increased by a factor of 4.5 relative to quiet-time levels. However, DTM2020, JB2008, NRLMSIS 2.0, and TIEGCM2.0 all underestimated the magnitude of this enhancement, with mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) values of 32.6%, 39.0%, 60.8%, and 40.6%, respectively. Coupling these models to the High Precision Orbit Propagator (HPOP) shows that the China Space Station (CSS) decay rates are 0.5–0.7 km/day during the main phase, about 2–3 times the quiet-time values. These predictions agree with Two-Line Element (TLE) derived semi-major axis decay trends, but significant magnitude discrepancies persist among different models, indicating that thermospheric model selection is a crucial uncertainty source in orbit prediction. A statistical analysis of Space-Track TLE data for LEO population (<1000 km) quantifies decay distribution across altitudes, providing direct references for space situational awareness and orbit maintenance strategies.

This paper offers a reflection centred on the synergy between Mindfulness-based Self-Awareness Workshops, Digital Storytelling and Generative Artificial Intelligence in contemporary educational contexts. The aim is to investigate the implications for students' individual and collective identity exploration processes and for the development of critical, reflective and emotionally oriented digital literacy. In this context, digital media and AI are not regarded as mere technical tools, nor as a shortcut to delegating thought to machines, but as a symbolic extension of the mind and body (Di Domenico et al., 2025), serving to enhance self-awareness and relational responsibility. The training programme is structured according to the perspective of Embodied Cognitive Science (ECS), recognising that cognition is deeply rooted in the body and influenced by emotional experience. (Gomez Paloma & Damiani, 2021; Varela et al., 1991). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 87-88. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Generative AI and New Narratives of the Self.

Material-level sensitivity or conductivity alone does not determine whether a wearable sensor produces trustworthy data. The signal must survive body coupling, packaging, wireless transfer, power constraints, and algorithmic interpretation. This cross-layer critical review examines six connected evidence streams: functional nanomaterial platforms, epidermal and implantable bioelectronic interfaces, wireless readout and power, integrated wearable platforms, artificial intelligence (AI)-based interpretation, and human-centred applications. Hysteresis and drift, interface instability, motion and environmental exposure, readout and power limits, placement and calibration dependence, and inter-user variability can degrade information across these layers. Robustness testing and claim-matched validation are needed to establish what the resulting outputs support. We therefore compare technologies through the failure modes and evidence requirements that persist after integration, rather than through isolated peak metrics. The synthesis offers conditional material-selection criteria for specific device roles, distinguishes demonstrated component functions from application-level claims, and identifies the reporting conditions and use-dependent validation priorities needed to interpret those claims.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

documents.abstract: Purpose This study examines how perceived generative AI literacy (GAIL) becomes employability-relevant for technical and vocational education and training (TVET) students through technological self-efficacy and career adaptability, and whether internship quality strengthens this pathway. Design/methodology/approach 526 Taiwanese TVET students with internship experience was analysed using standardised composite-score path analysis, 5,000-resample nonparametric bootstrapping, moderation tests and subgroup diagnostics. Findings All six hypotheses were supported. Perceived GAIL was positively associated with technological self-efficacy, career adaptability and perceived employability through the hypothesised serial pathway. Internship quality strengthened the first-stage association. Supplementary records linked perceived GAIL with task performance and supervisor ratings, and perceived employability with later employment and job fit. Research limitations/implications Although supplementary performance, rater, supervisor and follow-up records reduce sole dependence on self-report, the primary structural model remains observational and perception-based. Future research should pre-register performance assessments and test measurement invariance across TVET tracks. Practical implications TVET providers should teach GenAI literacy as responsible task performance, not mere tool use, and connect it to supervised internship tasks, feedback and transparent skill signalling. Originality/value The study specifies a GenAI-focused, theory-grounded employability pathway and identifies internship quality as a workplace-learning condition under which perceived digital competence is more strongly associated with career confidence.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the way individuals interact with digital technologies and Information Systems (IS), requiring a rethinking of some traditional assumptions underlying Human–Computer Interaction (HCI). In Management Information Systems (MIS), this transformation extends beyond the design of usable interfaces toward the development of intelligent systems that can actively support, augment, and collaborate with human users. This chapter examines the evolution from HCI to Human–AI Collaboration (HAC) and discusses its implications for the development of intelligent MIS. It first establishes the conceptual foundations of HCI, including human factors, user-centered design, usability, accessibility, and user experience (UX). It then examines the emergence of Human–AI Interaction (HAI) and the transition from computers as passive tools toward intelligent interaction partners. Building on this foundation, the chapter conceptualizes HAC through complementary human and AI capabilities, human oversight, AI-augmented decision-making, and increasingly autonomous AI systems. Particular attention is given to human-centered design, Generative AI, conversational and multimodal interfaces, intelligent UX, and the different roles humans may assume in AI-enabled environments, including interaction, evaluation, supervision, and, under appropriate conditions, collaboration with AI systems. The chapter further discusses ethical and organizational challenges, including algorithmic bias, privacy, transparency, accountability, automation bias, and human agency. It argues that the future of MIS will increasingly depend not only on technological intelligence but also on how effectively HAC is designed, governed, and integrated into organizational work.

Autonomous and AI-driven systems now issue operations whose consequences land far from where they were decided: in radio-access-network controllers, operator charging systems, device queues and DMA engines, robot actuators, emergency broadcast channels, payment rails, browsers, and long-running agent processes that migrate between hosts. Across all of these, a recurring failure appears. A system treats an acknowledgement, a status code, a callback, a log entry, or its own internal view as if it were proof that the intended effect occurred, on the intended target, under the conditions that were authorized. Observations are fused across mismatched clocks, identities, and configuration generations; agreements are treated as execution authority; partial effects are retried as if nothing happened; translated or transformed instructions are delivered as though they preserved their original meaning. This disclosure addresses that gap as a single architectural problem expressed across many domains. The disclosure presents a 280-page technical record comprising common-workflow flowcharts, phase-level engineering figures, implementation flowcharts, and 639 proposed patent claims. Its unifying principle is that the original authorized operation retains a stable identity from which every downstream representation, transformation, dispatch, acknowledgement, and observed effect must be separately reconstructed and qualified. Each workflow applies a conservative three-valued rule at every gate: all mandatory predicates supported advances; any predicate contradicted inhibits or raises an exception; any predicate unresolved holds. Final outcomes are expressed as scoped verdicts (CONSISTENT, INCONSISTENT, or UNRESOLVED) with the evidence, resource state, and gaps on which each verdict depends. Throughout, acknowledgement is distinguished from effect, observation from authority, eligibility from authorization, and historical records from current permission. The record is organized into technical groups, each with its own common workflow and claim set: Group A (claims 1–40) governs observation-to-control consistency in radio-access-network calculations: reconstructing resource identity and configuration generation, bounding temporal applicability under clock uncertainty, preserving measurement semantics across interfaces, selecting dependency-aware joint observations, maintaining consistency through controller migration and failover, and revalidating material dependencies before a control result is delivered. Group B (claims 41–80) addresses multi-agent network incident diagnosis and repair, covering source-qualified evidence provenance and independence, competing fault hypotheses resolved by discriminating evidence, repair-plan applicability under concurrent changes, asynchronous repair with partial-effect reconstruction, independent post-repair verification of recovery and adverse effects, and distributed incident history with recurrence analysis. Group C (claims 81–120) maintains telecommunications session lifecycle consistency across subscriber trust changes (SIM/eSIM), home and visited operator roaming and partial release, concurrent programmable quality-on-demand operations, user-plane usage, quota and charging lineage, purpose-scoped consent versus actual network effect, and partial operator outage with deferred settlement. Group D (claims 121–160) reconstructs hardware observation-to-effect consistency through independent hardware observers, CPU-to-device DMA memory continuity, device queue and descriptor occupancy, firmware and configuration invalidation, and cross-stage representation of external effects. Group E (claims 161–200) holds that negotiated agreement is not execution authority among multiple agents, covering versioned negotiation and partial acceptance, streaming artifacts and delegated sub-actions, amendment impact across versions, cancellation and late effects, partitioned participant views, and residual obligations at closure. Group F (claims 201–240) treats asynchronous tool and protocol operations, including durable task identity and callback origin, tool-schema generation and in-flight semantic change, acknowledged subscription and push-event coverage, resource alias and generation continuity, cancellation and retry with residual external effects, and concurrent usage-budget settlement. Group G (claims 241–280) translates machine-readable robot skills into calibration-qualified physical capability, evaluated by an independent safety controller, admitted under time-bounded command contracts, downgraded at runtime when capability degrades mid-actuation, transferred between robots without reusing unverified calibration, and closed by independent physical-effect observation. Group H (claims 281–320) carries emergency instructions from source to physical response: original instruction identity and provenance, extraction and preservation of safety-critical meaning, multilingual translation verification under uncertainty, recipient-specific exact-content dispatch, correction and supersession, and readback and response verification. Group M1 (claims 321–380) governs autonomous AI commerce from original purchase intent to actual commercial outcome, covering product, variant and seller continuity, complete monetary exposure at dynamic checkout, current purchasing authority, payment-mandate-to-financial-effect consistency, multi-agent shared budgets, and post-purchase fulfilment, refund, and correction. Group M2 (claims 381–440) operates at silicon level, binding an authorized operation to the hardware command a device actually consumes, through descriptor integrity, effective DMA translation and invalidation, reset and assignment incarnation, protected command admission with atomic use-state, shared quota admission, and cross-path effectuation coverage. Claims 441–509 extend the architecture to protected virtual-machine and sandbox runtimes with consequence-bound egress, dual-boundary digital-to-physical command enforcement, controller-local authority without transferable tokens, protected credential release, buffered physical-command invalidation, crash-resistant authority recovery, authority preservation across checkpoint, fork, migration and changing delegation, and separation of informative context from consequential execution. Group I (claims 510–539, with 600–639) secures browser and graphical-agent actions by binding an authorized task to the actual interface target, frame, origin, redirect, and background request it produces, and extends this to interface-independent control across graphical, voice, remote, native, and terminal interfaces. Group J (claims 540–599, with 600–639) preserves a persistent agent task’s logical identity, authority, outstanding external exposure, and callbacks across migration between execution instances, using generation fencing, representation-independent current authority, and callback-independent outcome verification, including treatment of partial and streaming effects without duplicate repetition. The material is offered as a public technical disclosure and reference architecture. The claims are proposed, not granted, and the figures describe implementation designs rather than guarantees of novelty, freedom to operate, or regulatory compliance. Safety-related content, including robotic and emergency-communication workflows, is non-certified and makes no SIL, PL, or standards-conformance claim. The record is intended for system architects, network and hardware engineers, AI-agent developers, standards contributors, and regulators concerned with accountable autonomy, where the question is not only whether an action was permitted, but whether what actually happened corresponds to what was authorized. Keywords: execution finality; intent-to-effect consistency; three-valued verification; autonomous agents; agentic AI governance; RAN observation consistency; telecom session lifecycle; network incident repair; hardware DMA integrity; silicon-level authorization; robotic capability verification; emergency instruction translation; agentic commerce; payment mandate; MCP asynchronous tools; browser agent security; agent migration; callback continuity; accountable autonomy

Transfer advising is a high-uncertainty setting where students rarely ask well-structured questions and advisors must infer intent from fragmented narratives across conflicting institutional policies. This research presents a human-centered AI framework that transforms naturalistic student discourse into structured advising intents, supporting a student-facing advising assistant whose explainable outputs are designed to support advisor review. Using 19,668 transfer-related Reddit posts, it surfaces recurring advising intents via extraction, clustering, and structured labeling, then routes student questions to them. On a proof-of-concept benchmark it reached 90% intent-level and 86% question-level accuracy, turning advising knowledge into transparent structures that support scalable, human-centered advising.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: In the contemporary landscape, an epistemological and educational crisis is becoming increasingly apparent, affecting the ways in which knowledge is produced and legitimised (Quattrociocchi, 2023). Learning is gradually moving away from the notion of a slow, dialogical process based on the accumulation of experience, and is taking on the characteristics of rapid, performance-oriented acquisition (Allouche, 2024). The educational relationship is also affected by this transformation, as the links that have long ensured consistency in educational processes are becoming weaker (Lingua & Zamengo, 2025). The erosion of mediation processes diminishes recognition of their value in the construction of knowledge and the formation of the individual. The authority of teachers and experts is facing a crisis of legitimacy, whilst algorithmic systems are increasingly perceived as reliable and impartial sources of knowledge. Similar dynamics are also at play in the realm of relationships and emotions. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 273-274. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Digital Affective Literacy and Citizenship.

Organisations make consequential decisions — product launches, pricing, policy changes — on behalf of populations they cannot observe directly. Two technologies promise to close this gap: people-data infrastructure, which indexes who individuals are, and generative population simulation, which uses large language model (LLM) agents to predict how people will respond. We argue that neither, alone or combined as currently practised, yields reliable decision intelligence. We identify seven gaps: coverage bias toward online, English-speaking, Western populations; unclear consent and provenance of grounding data; reliance on stated rather than revealed behaviour; static rather than temporal modelling; individuals simulated without social networks; the absence of decision-level evaluation standards; and a missing link between predicted reactions and the decision a firm must take. We propose a four-layer architecture — a consented, predictive people layer; a twin engine; a simulation runtime; and a decision layer — and an evaluation agenda based on back-testing against historical outcomes. We show that because decisions are comparisons, shared model bias and individual noise largely cancel, leaving option-specific cultural bias as the error that matters most. This is a position paper. It reports no new experiments; figures in Section 6 are explicitly assumed planning targets, not findings. AI writing tools assisted in drafting; the author reviewed and takes responsibility for the content.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In increasingly complex and technology-rich educational environments, teachers are expected not only to master instructional strategies but also to critically interpret educational situations and make pedagogically informed decisions. Professional reflection has therefore become a fundamental component of teacher education, enabling educators to connect experience with pedagogical action (Dewey, 1933; Schön, 1983; Mortari, 2003). Within this perspective, the reflective journal functions as a self-narrative pedagogical device through which teachers reinterpret classroom situations, strengthening professional judgement and inclusive educational decision-making. From a narrative perspective, reflection transforms experience into meaning (Bruner, 1992). Digital storytelling has also been recognised as an effective strategy for fostering reflection and professional learning (Robin, 2008; Banzato, 2014; De Marco & Colazzo, 2021; Mazzini et al., 2025). At the same time, recent research has highlighted both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for its pedagogically grounded integration into teacher education (Holmes et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2025). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 74-76. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Generative AI and New Narratives of the Self.

Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education is rapidly reshaping learning and assessment, offering unprecedented opportunities for creativity, personalization, and efficiency. This chapter explores the complex nexus between AI, creativity, and assessment. The SAMR model (i.e., substitution, augmentation, modification, and redefinition) is applied to examine how AI is utilized across a spectrum of assessment practices, from substitution and augmentation to modification and redefinition. The findings show that although AI holds the potential to enhance creative thinking through adaptive learning and intelligent tutoring, it also elicits concerns regarding the potential for limiting originality, fostering cognitive dependency, and the mechanization of learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into nursing education, research, and practice, raising concerns about cultural relevance, ethical integrity, and preservation of human-centered care. To address these challenges, the Transcultural Nurse-Artificial Intelligence (TCN-AI) Synergy Model was developed. METHODS: Using Walker and Avant's theory derivation method, the model was derived from the Translation Validity Index. Core concepts were identified, redefined, and extended to explain the interaction between AI-generated outputs and transcultural nursing expertise. RESULTS: The model conceptualizes this interaction as an iterative process of appraisal, contextualization, and refinement. Also, the accompanying AI Output Evaluation Rubric was developed to systematically assess AI-generated content for cultural relevance, conceptual validity, ethical integrity, and clinical relevance across nursing education, research, and practice. DISCUSSION: The TCN-AI Synergy Model advances transcultural nursing theory, education, research, and practice by providing a practical framework for critically evaluating AI-generated outputs. The accompanying rubric potentially enables efficient, systematic assessment while supporting informed decision-making in academic, research, and clinical settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure preferences and opinions, but outputs vary across prompts, personas, and model checkpoints, leaving analysts with multiple noisy elicitation variants and no principled way to combine them. Existing practice typically relies on heuristic aggregation---uniform averaging, population-weighted post-stratification, or selecting the single best subgroup---which uses fixed ex ante weights and can remain misaligned with human benchmarks. We propose Human Mimicry Calibration (HuMCal), a post-hoc calibration method that learns credibility weights over elicitation variants using only aggregate benchmark data, with no access to model internals or subgroup-level labels. HuMCal is model-agnostic and baseline-safe on the calibration split: its optimized loss weakly dominates any fixed-weight rule over the same subgroup set, including uniform weighting, post-stratification, and the best single subgroup. We evaluate HuMCal in a revealed-preference market-structure application using U.S. bank-card transactions and in a public-opinion application using Pew survey data. Across both settings, HuMCal improves alignment on the calibration split relative to all fixed-weight baselines. Out of sample, source-learned weights outperform heuristic baselines across time, geography, industry, and topic in the large majority of evaluations, although transfer is empirical rather than guaranteed. Recalibration with newer LLM checkpoints often improves alignment further. These results suggest that HuMCal can serve as a scalable calibration tool for LLM-based measurement when collecting fresh benchmark data for each target setting is costly.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter explores the potential of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to provide fit-for-purpose assessments of product creativity in a classroom context. The chapter discusses the drivers behind the need for classroom creativity assessment and focuses on the factors central to the fitness-for-purpose of creativity assessments, including quality, logistics, and authenticity. The chapter then explores these issues through a custom GPT in the OpenAI/ChatGPT large language model (LLM) environment. The custom GPT is tested (a) to explore its ability to provide meaningful summative evaluations (i.e., numerical scores) of creativity (by comparing the custom GPT scores with human evaluations of creative writing and mousetrap designs) and (b) to explore its ability to provide meaningful formative feedback (by examining its evaluation of different paper airplane designs). The chapter concludes by suggesting that generative AI (specifically LLMs) has good potential to address long-standing issues of the fitness-for-purpose of classroom creativity assessments. In the era of Industry 4, and the rise of creativity as an essential 21st-century skill, the ability to assess creativity in the classroom is the key to ensuring that students are prepared for the challenges of the future of work.

Purpose This study aims to explore the impact of organizational technology strategies, particularly in the context of artificial intelligence (AI), on employees’ daily job activities. It also looks at the extent of the transformation and the role of leadership, supportive of innovation and cultural change, in reinforcing the transformation. Design/methodology/approach The researcher adopted a quantitative research design based on the survey data collected from employees in various industries in Pakistan. The researcher used structural equation modeling to analyze the relationships among technology strategies, organizational facilitators and the transformation of job roles. Findings The research shows that organizations that implement AI and automation alongside digitized processes and advanced data analysis capabilities will experience fundamental changes in their employees’ work functions, skills and job duties. The implementation of digital strategies enhances operational efficiency, but their impact extends beyond this benefit, as they completely transform how work is executed. The presence of an innovation-supportive culture together with strong leadership commitment creates an enhanced effect. The combination of encouragement of organizational experimentation and active leadership support for technological change results in more visible and positive changes in job responsibilities. Practical implications The research findings demonstrate that organizations need to combine technology investments with operational changes to achieve successful digital transformation outcomes. Organizations must establish supportive cultures together with proactive leadership to assist employees throughout the process of organizational change. Organizations need to develop their employees’ skills and build adaptable workforces while maintaining open communication to implement meaningful job role changes that last over time. Originality/value The research contributes to the future of work literature by examining how workers change their job functions at the individual-employee level rather than observing outcomes at the organizational level. The research describes how organizations use technology strategies and organizational enablers to create distinct work environments for the AI age by integrating Job Demands–Resources and Socio-Technical Systems perspectives.

Drug discovery remains a costly and time-consuming process, motivating the development of artificial intelligence approaches to accelerate molecular design. Many generative models, including generative pre-trained transformers (GPT), rely on one-dimensional SMILES representations that lack explicit structural topology and are constrained by rigid syntax rules. Moreover, most existing models perform unconditional molecule generation, while the few conditional diffusion approaches often rely on abstract parameters rather than pharmacologically interpretable constraints. Consequently, current methods have limited ability to enforce explicit drug-like and pharmacophore requirements during molecular generation. Here, we propose GCMDiff, a multi-condition guided diffusion framework for molecular graph generation that supports controllable and interpretable molecular design. Unlike SMILES-based models, GCMDiff employs an atom-pair and bond-centric molecular graph representation that directly captures explicit chemical topologies. Crucially, we introduce an interpretable pharmacological condition embedding that integrates multi-modal constraints, including atom number, Lipinski’s Rule of Five constraints, and structural moieties derived from Checkmol, PubChem, and Rings in Drugs descriptors. These explicit features guide the diffusion process toward promising chemical spaces satisfying user-defined prerequisites. Benchmark experiments demonstrate that GCMDiff generates chemically valid and structurally diverse molecules, achieving 99.6% novelty and 100% uniqueness while maintaining atom and bond distributions consistent with drug-like chemical space. As a practical application, GCMDiff was applied to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitor design, where generated candidates reproduced key binding interactions, including the conserved hydrogen bond between a quinazoline scaffold and residue Met793. These results demonstrate that GCMDiff provides a flexible and interpretable framework for pharmacophore-fragment-conditioned molecular generation, enabling controllable exploration of drug-like chemical space and facilitating early-stage rational drug discovery. Scientific contribution GCMDiff advances molecular design by employing a graph-based diffusion framework that bypasses SMILES-related syntax limitations. Its core innovation is a multi-modal condition encoder integrating drug-like properties and pharmacophores, enabling interpretable, pharmacophore-fragment-conditioned molecular generation. The model achieves 99.6% novelty and 100% uniqueness while demonstrating practical utility through the design of novel EGFR inhibitors that replicate essential Met793 binding interactions. This framework effectively bridges generative AI with rational, constraint-driven lead optimization.

The article addresses the topical issue of using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in working with academic texts by combining practical work with GenAI, the analysis of dissertation abstracts, and the development of students’ critical attitudes toward AI-generated information. This study investigates the ability of generative artificial intelligence to reconstruct selected conceptual components of academic discourse without direct access to the corresponding dissertation abstract. The study analyzes contemporary scholarly approaches to the use of generative artificial intelligence in academic discourse. The aim of the study is to empirically determine the extent to which GenAI can reproduce the relevance, research aim, and research focus of an academic study based on a minimal set of input data. The methodology involved an experimental procedure with 25 undergraduate students enrolled in the program “Language and Literature (German). Translation” within the field of Germanic languages and literatures. The empirical material comprised 25 abstracts of successfully defended dissertations on Germanic linguistics. Two generative AI systems, ChatGPT and Gemini, were used in the experiment. Following a standardized prompting procedure, the systems were provided with the research topic, but the corresponding dissertation abstract was not made available to them. The AI-generated responses were compared with the corresponding conceptual components of the dissertation abstracts using comparative content analysis. The results indicate that GenAI can semantically reconstruct selected characteristics of an existing academic study, including its relevance, research aim, and focus. At the same time, the findings do not indicate textual copying of dissertation abstracts but rather suggest the possibility of reconstructing their content-related characteristics from limited input data. These results indicate the considerable potential of GenAI as a tool for supporting academic writing. Practical implications. The findings may be used to develop university curricula that establish a balanced approach to integrating generative artificial intelligence into the educational process while preserving fundamental principles of academic integrity and values.

Addressing how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes the cognitive act of second language (L2) writing, this conceptual article draws on recent empirical literature (2023–2026). It grounds its analysis in the Cognitive Process Theory of Writing (CPTW), chosen because its decomposition of planning, translating, and reviewing under working-memory limits illuminates how cognitive labor is redistributed between learner and machine. Through CPTW, three key insights emerge. First, planning undergoes an externalization of productive struggle: offloading idea generation causes learners to bypass essential rhetorical problem framing. Second, translating experiences a voice constraint: model optimization toward conventionality flattens non-standard L2 syntax and homogenizes authorial voice. Third, reviewing suffers a reviewing bifurcation, splitting evaluation into goal-level appraisal and opaque decision-level monitoring. Theoretically, GenAI transforms writing into a co-generative sociotechnical practice requiring GenAI feedback literacy. Pedagogically, educators should adopt process-oriented assessments, using pre-prompting framing logs, annotated drafts, and prompt histories to evaluate cognitive engagement over polished final products.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping innovation management by moving beyond its conventional role as a technological tool toward becoming an active participant in creative and decision-making processes. This chapter examines how GenAI can function as a co-creator across the innovation process and explores the complementary roles of human and artificial intelligence in generating meaningful innovation outcomes. Adopting a structured integrative literature review approach, the study synthesizes recent research on GenAI-enabled innovation through thematic analysis and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate that GenAI contributes across multiple stages of innovation, including opportunity recognition, idea generation and evaluation, product and service development, business model innovation, commercialization, and organizational innovation. Its primary strengths lie in rapid content generation, knowledge synthesis, recombination, scenario development, and iterative refinement, whereas human contributors remain central to problem framing, contextual interpretation, strategic and ethical judgment, validation, and accountability. Building on these complementary capabilities, the chapter proposes the Human–GenAI Innovation Co-Creation Framework, which conceptualizes innovation as an iterative cycle of framing, generating, evaluating, refining, validating, and experimenting. The analysis further identifies hallucination, bias and idea homogenization, intellectual property concerns, human over-reliance, AI literacy, and organizational governance as important boundary conditions shaping the effectiveness of co-creation. Overall, the chapter argues that the transformative potential of GenAI in innovation management lies not in replacing human innovators but in designing organizational processes that deliberately combine human judgment and creativity with GenAI’s generative and synthetic capabilities.

Abstract This study examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve university students’ mathematical problem-solving when it is designed not as an answer generator but as a metacognitive scaffold. Building on sociocultural scaffolding, self-regulated learning, and Pólya’s problem-solving model, the study tested a 15-week structured GenAI-supported intervention in Calculus I. A cluster-assigned quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was implemented with 128 undergraduates distributed across four tutorial sections: two sections used a Socratic GenAI protocol (n = 60), and two sections received traditional instruction using the same weekly problem sets (n = 68). Students’ solutions were scored with a validated analytic rubric aligned with the four Pólya stages, and outcomes were analyzed using ANCOVA with pre-test adjustment and a multilevel sensitivity model for section-level clustering. Results showed a statistically significant adjusted between-group difference favoring the GenAI-supported group, F(1, 125) = 28.76, p < .001, partial eta squared = .187, with the largest stage-specific effects for carrying out the plan and understanding the problem. Student perceptions were highly positive, and cognitive engagement showed the strongest association with performance gains. The study contributes to educational psychology by specifying a testable instructional mechanism: structured GenAI-supported instruction may support mathematical problem solving when prompts elicit planning, monitoring, explanation, and reflection while discouraging direct solution-seeking.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid rise of generative AI (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for fostering creativity in kindergarten through Grade 12 (K–12) education. This systematic scoping review analyzes 45 studies (2017–2025) to examine how GenAI is applied in creative learning. The chapter identifies four main categories: creativity assessment, human–AI co-creativity, stakeholders’ perceptions, and creativity enhancement. Findings reveal a dominant focus on language-based tasks such as storytelling, with limited attention to auditory, embodied, or spatial creativity. Although GenAI tools show potential in supporting idea generation, multimodal expression, and co-creation, most studies lack theoretical grounding and comprehensive assessment methods. Frameworks such as the 4C model or evidence-centered design are rarely used, and equity concerns—such as access, cultural representation, and student agency—remain underexplored. Although emerging GenAI tools enable personalized feedback and formative assessment, they also raise questions about authorship transparency and ethical use. This chapter provides a foundation for advancing equitable and responsible integration of GenAI to support creativity in K–12 education. It advocates for ethically grounded, theory-informed, and developmentally appropriate GenAI designs that enhance rather than automate creativity.

documents.abstract: Introduction The widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in knowledge-intensive domains requires continuous adjustment of human cognitive patterns. In terminology work, aligning strict semantic standards against the non-deterministic output of large language models (LLMs) is closely intertwined with workers' subjective cognitive load. This study examines the structural associations among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load, while testing the potential moderating role of professional experience. Methods Based on cross-sectional survey data from 1,760 practitioners using LLMs for terminology tasks, structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) were employed. SEM evaluated the linear structural associations among prompt strategy preference, self-efficacy, and cognitive load, while LPA identified behavioral user profiles. Multi-group equivalence testing was further conducted across three career stages (novices, intermediates, and experts). Results Prompt strategy preference is significantly and negatively associated with subjective cognitive load, with AI interaction self-efficacy serving as a significant mediator in this structural relationship. LPA identified three distinct user profiles (low, medium, and high strategy use), with the high strategy group exhibiting the lowest cognitive load and highest self-efficacy. Multi-group equivalence tests indicated no statistically significant moderation across experience cohorts, demonstrating structural invariance of the core model across career stages. Discussion From the perspective of cognitive ergonomics, upfront prompt structuring is structurally linked to downstream cognitive offloading and psychological buffering. These findings provide empirical evidence for individual cognitive resilience during human-AI collaboration in the generative AI era.

documents.abstract: Emerging remote sensing technologies increasingly support coastal observation through Earth observation (EO) derivatives such as satellite-derived shorelines, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)- and light detection and ranging (LiDAR)-based elevation models, coastal land-use/land-cover products, bathymetric grids, turbidity and chlorophyll-a indicators, habitat maps, flood extents, and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated segmentation outputs. These EO-derived products are central to shoreline monitoring, coastal vulnerability assessment, flood-response planning, marine ecosystem management, and land–sea administration. Yet their evidential value depends on transparent provenance: users must know which sensor, acquisition condition, preprocessing chain, algorithm, model version, validation dataset, and uncertainty estimate produced each coastal product. The review synthesises 156 eligible publications identified through a systematic review process. Of these, 89 studies containing sufficient implementation and methodological detail were selected for detailed analytical coding. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol, the review analyses application domains, provenance capture modes, representation strategies, semantic web technologies, and interoperability practices. A coastal EO thematic refinement translates the review findings into provenance requirements for satellite, UAV, LiDAR, Internet of Things (IoT), open-water, and AI-enabled coastal observation workflows. The review identifies persistent gaps in feature-level lineage, alignment between the World Wide Web Consortium Provenance Ontology (PROV-O) and International Organization for Standardization (ISO) geospatial metadata standards, spatial semantics, AI workflow transparency, uncertainty traceability, and scalable querying. To address these limitations, the paper introduces GeoPROV, a lightweight semantic profile of PROV-O designed for spatially explicit, feature-level provenance. GeoPROV aligns PROV-O with ISO 19115/19157, GeoSPARQL, Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), and SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogue (STAC)-compatible catalogue practices. The framework enables EO-derived coastal products to be traced from raw observation through preprocessing, AI/geoprocessing, validation, catalogue publication, and coastal-administrative decision-making. The resulting GeoPROV profile integrates PROV-O, GeoSPARQL, SHACL, ISO 19115/19157 lineage concepts, and STAC metadata within a lightweight semantic framework demonstrated through a coastal EO product workflow and machine-actionable provenance implementation.

BACKGROUND: Low back pain (LBP) remains a leading cause of disability worldwide. However, the disease burden among people aged 15-49 years has been insufficiently addressed. OBJECTIVE: The present study aimed to investigate the global burden, temporal trends, and attributable risk factors of low back pain among people aged 15-49 years. METHODS: Using data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study 2021, we analyzed the incidence, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) of LBP across 204 countries and territories. Age-standardized rates (ASRs) were calculated, and temporal trends from 1990 to 2021 were examined using joinpoint regression. RESULTS: According to GBD 2021 estimates, there are approximately 16,993,809 new cases of LBP that occurred worldwide, with South Asia bearing the highest case load. Although ASRs of incidence (AAPC: -0.16; 95% CI: -0.20, -0.12), ASRs of prevalence (AAPC: -0.17; 95% CI: -0.20, -0.14), and ASRs of DALYs (AAPC: -0.16; 95% CI: -0.18, -0.14) declined between 1990 and 2021, absolute case numbers and DALYs increased. Occupational ergonomic factors (28.4%, 95% CI: 26.3%-30.7%), tobacco smoking (11.4%, 95% CI: 7.6%-15.2%), and high body mass index (BMI) (10.9%, 95% CI: 1.1%-21.0%) were the major attributable risk factors. Women always bear a more severe disease burden than men, with the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) being 3788.64 vs. 2380.94 per 100,000; the age-standardized prevalence rate (ASPR) being 8822.52 vs. 5410.51 per 100,000; and the age-standardized DALY rates (ASDR) being 999.13 vs. 626.28 per 100,000 in women and men, respectively. When it comes to the socio-demographic index (SDI), ASIR and ASPR initially increased with rising SDI, reaching a peak in Australasia, with ASPR over 12,500 per 100,000 and ASIR over 5000 per 100,000, before subsequently decreasing with further SDI increments. CONCLUSIONS: Despite declining ASRs, the absolute global burden of LBP among individuals aged 15-49 continues to grow, particularly among women and in high-SDI regions. Targeted preventive strategies and control measures are urgently needed.

Purpose: This study develops a governance architecture for board-governed strategic decisions in which artificial intelligence (AI) provides common advice while legal and organizational decision ownership remains human. It examines two linked risks: erosion of independent human information and distortion of delegation through outcome-dependent credit and blame. Methodology/Approach: A theoretical decision-economic model is used to formalize firm-optimal and executive-optimal delegation, an endogenous attribution wedge, common-AI-induced error covariance, and boundary conditions for pre-AI information recording. The analysis treats governance controls as ex-ante commitments rather than ex-post corrections. Findings: Common exposure to an imperfect AI signal can increase correlation among revised human judgments and reduce the effective number of independent checks. Separately, private attribution incentives can move delegation away from the firm-optimal benchmark. The proposed Information Lock records designated human assessments before common AI exposure, while the Accountability Lock fixes effective decision rights and attribution rules before outcomes are known. The model also identifies limits: perfectly reconstructible post-AI judgments reduce the Information Lock mainly to an auditability device, while residual career downside can shift distortion from over-delegation toward rejection or delay of positive-value decisions. Conclusion: The contribution is a unified, selective governance architecture linking information independence and outcome-invariant accountability. It provides boards and senior executives with an implementable framework for preserving informational diversity, clarifying decision ownership, and distinguishing poor process from unfavorable stochastic outcomes in AI-assisted strategic decisions.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly discussed as a catalyst for transforming academic development by enabling more personalized, responsive, and collaborative professional learning. However, the research landscape remains fragmented across diverse themes and methodological approaches. This study provides a bibliometric and thematic synthesis of AI-related research relevant to academic development, focusing on personalized learning, adaptive feedback, and collaborative growth. Using a systematic review protocol informed by PRISMA and PICO frameworks, 507 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2024 were identified from major academic databases. Bibliometric analysis examined publication trends, thematic clusters, and methodological patterns, followed by a qualitative synthesis of findings related to academic development outcomes. The results indicate three dominant directions. First, AI-driven personalization is widely reported as supporting tailored learning pathways and just-in-time instructional support. Second, adaptive feedback systems, including intelligent tutoring systems and automated analytics tools, are associated with improvements in instructional decision-making and pedagogical reflection. Third, AI-supported collaborative environments are emerging as mechanisms for peer learning, mentorship, and knowledge exchange. Adoption remains uneven, with barriers including ethical concerns, digital readiness, and varying faculty acceptance. Overall, AI technologies hold significant potential to enhance academic development when integrated with institutional support, ethical governance, and context-sensitive implementation strategies.
