documents.abstract: Background: COVID-19 has globally challenged health systems and created profound psychosocial consequences for healthcare workers. Hopelessness, as a negative future expectation, may emerge alongside fear, anxiety, and burnout. This study aimed to examine hopelessness levels among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and to identify associated factors based on their experiences and perceptions.Methods: The research group consisted of all employees at an education and research hospital. Data were collected from 562 personnel (48.2% of active staff). The data collection tools included a questionnaire and the Beck Hopelessness Scale. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni/Tamhane post-hoc tests, and stepwise multiple linear regression model.Results: The mean age was 35.8±8.8 years, and the mean length of service was 9.1±8.3 years. Of the participants, 61.2% were female, 30.8% were doctors, and 27.0% nurses. Nearly one-third had worked in COVID-19 units, one-third had been infected, and more than half had directly cared for COVID-19 patients. In bivariate analyses, smoking, workplace reassignment, direct care of patients with COVID-19, and perceiving colleagues’ knowledge as insufficient were associated with higher hopelessness. In the multivariable model, female gender, chronic illness or disability, a mixed work schedule, psychological impact, the belief that the pandemic could not be controlled, and pessimistic expectations about returning to normal life remained independently associated with hopelessness.Conclusion: Hopelessness is a critical psychological concern among healthcare workers in pandemic disasters. Early recognition of vulnerable groups and institutional support to reduce uncertainty, provide adequate Personal Protective Equipment, and regulate shift work are essential to strengthen workforce resilience. These findings highlight the need to integrate psychological well-being into pandemic preparedness and occupational health policies.

Background As climate concerns intensify and artificial intelligence transforms retail experiences, understanding how AI tools influence sustainable consumption decisions has become increasingly critical. This study investigates how AI-assisted shopping affects consumer purchase intentions for plant-based proteins—a key lever for dietary sustainability—by examining the mediating roles of perceived usefulness and trust in AI technology. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, we propose that AI usage and environmental concern influence purchase intentions through dual cognitive and affective pathways. Method We test this framework using survey data from 519 Amazon customers in the United States, analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The measurement model demonstrates excellent psychometric properties, with all constructs exceeding recommended thresholds for reliability and validity. Results The study reveals that both AI usage and environmental concern significantly enhance perceived usefulness of AI for sustainability decisions and trust in AI recommendations, which subsequently drive plant-based protein purchase intentions. The effects operate entirely through these mediating mechanisms, with perceived usefulness showing stronger influence than trust. The model explains 22.4% of variance in purchase intentions, indicating substantial explanatory power for behavioral research. These findings advance theoretical understanding of AI-mediated sustainable consumption while offering practical guidance for e-commerce platforms and marketers. Conclusions The study demonstrates that digital technologies can facilitate environmental behavior change when consumers perceive them as both useful for achieving sustainability goals and trustworthy in their recommendations, particularly among environmentally conscious consumers.

Physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour represent one of the most pressing global health challenges of the twenty-first century. Insufficient physical activity is causally associated with noncommunicable diseases, mental health disorders, and premature mortality (Bull et al., 2020; WHO, 2022). Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising avenue for promoting physical activity at scale: AI-powered tools can deliver personalised coaching, adaptive training plans, real-time feedback, and behavioural nudges in ways that traditional interventions cannot replicate (Guerriero et al., 2026). However, the landscape of AI tools for physical activity is highly heterogeneous and research remains fragmented, with no comprehensive functional mapping of tools available to end users. This chapter addresses that gap. This contribution draws on an exploratory mapping study in which AI tools for physical activity promotion were identified through systematic navigation of There's an AI for That a directory indexing over 50,000 AI tools. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 397-398. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Kinesiology and sport between education and performance in European area.

The growing professionalisation of influencers has intensified tensions surrounding authenticity, yet little is known about how audiences perceive and respond to it. This study examines how audiences interpret professionalisation through organisational cues and navigate the authenticity tensions these cues evoke, taking the Multi-Channel Network disclosure on Chinese social media as an empirical case. Based on 20 in-depth interviews, findings show that audiences interpret the disclosure as a symbol of professionalisation, which implies technical expertise and corporatised operation. Using a multidimensional authenticity framework, professionalisation is perceived to diminish influencers’ intrinsic motivation and honesty. However, rather than rejecting professionalised influencers, audiences negotiate authenticity loss by normalising professionalisation, setting boundaries of acceptance, and prioritising content usefulness and entertainment. These negotiation practices enable audiences to reconcile tensions between professionalisation and authenticity and sustain engagement with professionalised influencers.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Geoffrey Hinton — often called the "Godfather of Artificial Intelligence" — has openly criticized Noam Chomsky, raising profound questions about the relationship between linguistics and artificial intelligence. This paper examines four dimensions along which large language models challenge established linguistic paradigms. First, should linguistics pursue a macro or micro-orientation? This debate concerns both the scope of linguistic inquiry and the transformation of its research methods; the paper argues that linguistics must shift from a narrow, discipline-confined perspective toward a comprehensive, interdisciplinary "macro-linguistics" that integrates with the humanities, natural sciences, medicine, and engineering, and that spans phonetics, grammar, semantics, and pragmatics. Second, are language and thought separable or inseparable? Contrary to the traditional dichotomy, this paper argues that human thought cannot be entirely separated from language: the primary purpose of thought is communication, and without new information, thought loses its vitality — artificial attempts to disconnect thought from communication are therefore counterproductive. Third, is language acquisition innate or experiential? Artificial intelligence has significantly challenged Chomsky's innateness hypothesis, abandoning the premise that language is a pre-programmed, innate ability in favor of treating language as fundamentally experiential — a shift validated by the landmark successes of experience-based learning models. Fourth, can AI possess thought, or even constitute life? The paper argues that artificial intelligence cannot possess life in the biological sense: AI's language is fundamentally disconnected from genuine thought, linguistic fluency does not equate to autonomous thinking, and AI remains an incomplete imitation of human language and cognition rather than an autonomous thinking entity.

Universities depend on staff contributions that exceed formal duties, such as sharing teaching practices, supporting students beyond scheduled hours, and volunteering for curriculum and quality-assurance work, to sustain teaching, research, and student support. University social responsibility (USR) is enacted largely through these same staff. Yet it remains unclear when staff perceptions of USR strengthen such discretionary contributions and when they are experienced as additional, unrecognized demands. This theory-synthesis article integrates USR, micro-level corporate social responsibility, organizational behavior, and recent higher education research to explain how perceived USR may translate into organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) among academic and administrative staff. Two pathways are proposed. A relational pathway links perceived USR to organizational justice, grounded in workload allocation, teaching assignments, promotion, and participation in decisions, and then to organizational trust, work engagement, and OCB. A motivational pathway links perceived USR to intrinsic motivation, engagement, and OCB when responsibility-related academic activities support autonomy and competence. Perceived organizational support is proposed to strengthen the relationship between perceived USR and organizational trust. Eight numbered propositions (P1-P8) are developed; Proposition 7 contains two constituent serial pathways (P7a and P7b). OCB is differentiated by its target: colleagues, students, and the institution. The framework identifies professional autonomy, collegial norms, role type, and workload systems as conditions that shape these relationships. Implications concern aligning USR commitments with fair academic workload, supportive practices, and recognized voluntary collaboration that benefits teaching and the learning environment.

Abstract This chapter examines human creativity in artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted learning through the lens of student agency. It first reviews four theoretical perspectives on agency—instrumental, effortful, dynamically emergent, and authorial—and analyzes how each perspective frames the relationship between learner agency and creativity. Building on this synthesis, the chapter discusses how generative AI (GenAI) reshapes students’ cognitive, social, and creative participation by extending their capabilities; redistributing agency across human–AI interactions; and raising new questions about authorship, responsibility, and ethical engagement. The chapter then introduces the framework of agentic engagement with AI, which conceptualizes learner agency as a proactive, adaptable, and reciprocal process enacted through the ongoing negotiation between human intentionality and machine adaptivity. This framework is further linked to mini-c creativity, highlighting how students use GenAI to construct personally meaningful ideas, interpretations, and creative expressions. Together, these perspectives shift attention from creativity as a product or performance outcome to a process of agentic meaning-making. The chapter concludes by proposing future research directions on the processes and outcomes of creativity in AI-assisted learning.

Purpose: This study examines the ethical and professional implications of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into clinical and community Social Work and its application within military settings, focusing on algorithmic bias, AI assisted data synthesis, privacy, and the preservation of human judgment. Research Methodology: The study adopts a qualitative documentary research design that draws on peer reviewed literature, professional standards, international policy documents, and relevant national frameworks. The documents were analyzed thematically through the lenses of Human Centered Design Theory, Sociotechnical Systems Theory, and the Social Justice Perspective. Results: AI offers opportunities to improve assessment, documentation, psychosocial intervention, research, and organizational decision making, but it raises serious concerns about privacy, confidentiality, informed consent, accountability, algorithmic bias, and transparency. These concerns intensify in military settings, where AI systems may process highly sensitive personal, health, and operational information about personnel, veterans, and their families. Conclusions: AI should be treated as a professional support technology rather than a substitute for Social Work judgment, therapeutic relationships, or accountable institutional decision making. Responsible adoption requires institutional safeguards, professional competencies, continuous auditing, meaningful human oversight, and mechanisms through which affected people can challenge AI supported decisions. Limitations: The study relies on secondary documents, does not test specific AI systems empirically, and focuses mainly on the Nigerian policy context. Contributions: The study proposes a Human Centered AI Framework for Social Work and Military Practice (HCAI SWMP) built on ethical governance, bias aware data management, secure data synthesis, and human centered implementation.

documents.abstract: Abstract A conceptual framework for understanding the intersection of human creativity and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education is presented in this chapter. The creative GenAI confluence framework offers a holistic perspective, serving as a lens to examine both how GenAI is used in educational contexts and its impact on human creativity and learning. Rather than viewing human creative processes and GenAI tools as merely additive, the framework conceptualizes their relationship as a complex, dynamic, and often reciprocal process, in which human and AI contributions are deeply intertwined and difficult to disentangle. This framework may support understanding common patterns of GenAI use in education and inform future research and practice across kindergarten through grade 12 and higher education settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Abstract: This chapter examines the dual role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in augmenting and challenging human creativity, particularly within higher education contexts. Through a synthesis of contemporary literature, it explores how AI democratizes creative expression by providing advanced tools to a broad audience while also addressing concerns over overreliance, equitable access, authorship, and cognitive development. The discussion focuses on how AI-driven workflows can support divergent thinking and bolster students’ creative confidence, with structured co-creation processes that enhance rather than replace human agency. Practical challenges—such as technical infrastructure, educator preparedness, and the adaptation of assessment practices for AI-assisted work—are also reviewed. By offering a comprehensive overview of AI’s evolving influence on creativity, the chapter highlights future opportunities and ethical and cultural considerations, ultimately providing insights for researchers, educators, and policymakers seeking to navigate the shifting intersection of AI, creativity, and education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university EFL students for language learning and academic tasks, yet fluent output may be inaccurate. This study examined self-reported trust and verification practices and students’ judgments of selected AI-generated English content among undergraduates at the Faculty of Languages, Surman, University of Sabratha. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was applied to questionnaire responses from 38 students. The instrument included background questions, ten five-point Likert items, five evaluation tasks with confidence and verification-intention responses, and an optional open-ended item. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Spearman’s rank correlations were used. Mean self-reported trust was 3.36/5 and verification was 3.74/5. Students correctly judged 62.1% of task responses under the primary answer key. Use frequency was not significantly associated with trust (ρ = .279, p = .090), whereas verification was associated with accuracy (ρ = .473, p = .003), as was confidence (ρ = .648, p < .001). Findings are preliminary given the small sample, modest trust-scale internal consistency, and ambiguity in one evaluation item. In exploratory HC3 regression, confidence remained associated with accuracy (β = .51, p = .005), while reported verification did not uniquely reach p < .05 after confidence was included (p = .063). After Holm correction across 28 exploratory pairs, only confidence–accuracy and awareness–adaptive-trust correlations remained significant. The study highlights the value of teaching verification and interpreting trust relative to output reliability.

The progressive integration of artificial intelligence into educational contexts is reshaping approaches to instructional mediation, the personalisation of learning pathways, and interaction with students. These potential applications are particularly relevant within the field of social and emotional learning (Goleman, 2011), especially for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), for whom structured and predictable learning environments characterised by gradual progression may foster the development of emotional and relational competencies. However, the use of generative artificial intelligence systems requires careful consideration of the implications associated with content reliability, process transparency, and the attribution of educational responsibility (Floridi, 2022). Indeed, the fluency and apparent plausibility of AI-generated responses do not guarantee their accuracy. Human supervision and validation processes are therefore essential to ensure that the content produced is scientifically grounded, pedagogically appropriate, and consistent with the intended learning objectives. documents.abstract: Generative AI is becoming part of technical communication workflows, but programs still need a grounded way to teach students how to use it while preserving rhetorical judgment, editorial responsibility, and audience awareness. This article proposes a human-in-the-loop pedagogy that treats AI as a system whose outputs must be defined, guided, evaluated, and constrained by human writers. It offers a heuristic for integrating AI into writing instruction while reinforcing the field’s core competencies.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has played a role in life sciences research and healthcare delivery for decades, though its nature and applications have changed with each new technology. As early as the 1950s, symbolic logic models provided clinical decision support: a form of deterministic AI encoded human knowledge as rules that an AI logic model could follow and implement (Nawaz et al., 2025). These early rule-based systems highlighted both the promise and limitations of symbolic AI. Subsequent periods of over-expectation followed by underdelivery contributed to recurring "AI winters" in which investment and enthusiasm declined.After 2010, computational and algorithmic developments led to machine learning (ML) and deep learning models. While these performed extremely well in some use cases (Habehh and Gohel, 2021), notably in biomedical research and image analysis, their use remained largely concentrated among technical experts and specialized applications. In the 2020s, large language models (LLMs) have rapidly changed the AI landscape in life sciences and medicine, and we are on the cusp of even faster evolutions, with state space models and active inference-based concepts that could lead to non-linear, novel leaps.The adoption of LLMs has been unlike that of any other modern technology. Most innovations, such as cars, mobile phones, and the internet, have taken years (between 1 year and 75 years) to reach adoption by 50 million users globally (Desjardins, 2018), whereas ChatGPT took only 5 days to achieve this. This unprecedented uptake leads to a paradigm shift in how we think about the users, use cases, and impact of a new technology. LLMs could change working practices in nearly every industry, to varying degrees. In their lead article, Guni et al. articulate the potential influence of LLMs in life sciences research and healthcare delivery (Guni et al. 2026). They review the rise and fall of AI applications in biomedical research and clinical decision support, and robustly discuss the elements needed for the current wave of AI to succeed. Specifically, they comment that "multidisciplinary effort (is needed) across several key domains: i) algorithmic science and architectures, ii) datasets, iii) processing power and efficiency, iv) infrastructure, v) human factors through codesign, and vi) interoperability with both legacy and modern healthcare systems." These efforts will require collaboration between clinicians, researchers, technologists, patients, ethicists, policymakers and others, and Guni et al. discuss a thorough breadth and depth of key topics. However, a seventh critical domain underlies all the others: the transformation of biomedical education and workforce development. Without a workforce capable of effectively leading AI systems, even the most sophisticated algorithms, datasets, and infrastructure will fail to deliver lasting impact, and we risk another AI winter.With respect to education, the widespread yet heterogenous use of LLMs by students and professors alike is challenging current pedagogy and assessment frameworks. In some cases, students are using LLMs to study or complete homework assignments, yet their professors lack expertise and are unprepared to alter their syllabus, homework, or exams (Lelescu et al 2025). In other cases, faculty are trying to integrate LLMs but are being met by significant resistance by students (Farinosi and Melchior, 2025). LLMs are also changing the day-to-day activities of our workforce, where adoption is similarly mixed and there is limited infrastructure to support broad, comprehensive workforce development. Many proposed educational responses focus primarily on the development of AI competencies across the continuum of learners and professionals. However, an exclusive focus on AI competencies introduces two related risks: "cognitive de-skilling", in which professionals gradually lose critical expertise and skills due to over-reliance on AI and "never-skilling", where the next generation of learners never fully develops foundational competencies because AI systems perform those tasks from the outset.Currently, health systems plan to measure the immediate augmented performance of AI tools in terms of clinical outcomes or immediate workflow efficiencies; we have yet to comprehensively measure their impact on retained competency or the longer-term implications of their use as a performance standard. Over the next 50 years, AI will likely become a critical part of many decision-making processes, training programs, and assessments done in clinical settings. However, if we never measure the retained competency of clinical staff to understand the impact of AI on long-term skill erosion, we could unintentionally introduce a critical system failure in the future. Clinicians who can no longer spot errors in AI tools or perform tasks when tools fail may put patients at risk and create a new type of AI winter-a systemic failure due to over-reliance on AI and lack of human competency. This AI winter would be extremely damaging to the practice of medicine in multiple ways: 1) direct risk to patients, 2) time to re-skill a generation of medical practitioners, and 3) lack of medical leaders with expertise to train the clinicians.Life sciences and healthcare are not the first knowledge-intensive domains to confront the challenge of maintaining human expertise as automation becomes increasingly capable. As commercial aviation systems evolved to automate key functions such as takeoff, landing, and navigation, concerns emerged that pilots were becoming overly reliant on automation, potentially eroding critical manual flying skills and reducing resilience when automated systems failed. Recognizing this risk, the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a Safety Alert in 2017 (FAA, 2017) and further guidance in 2022 (FAA, 2022) to strengthen policies and training that preserved pilot proficiency in manual operations.This experience provides a compelling parallel to the adoption of AI-driven clinical decision support systems. In both aviation and healthcare, humans and technology function as components of a sociotechnical system (Trist, 1981), where safety depends on the effective interaction between people, processes, and tools. When technological capabilities advance without corresponding attention to human competencies, organizations risk losing the very redundancies that protect against failure. The FAA's approach demonstrates that successful integration of automation requires more than technical performance; it requires deliberate governance, training, monitoring, and ongoing investment in human expertise. Ultimately, the safety of any automated system depends not only on the technology itself, but also on how human competency is preserved and strengthened alongside it (Macnamara et al., 2024).In short, humans must be the redundancy when technology systems fail.To avoid creating a generation of professionals who cannot function effectively when AI systems are unavailable, unreliable, or incorrect, we need radical transformation in our education and workforce development frameworks to teach both AI competencies and domain-specific competencies in synchrony. We must develop these competency frameworks now to prepare the future workforce to thrive in an AI-enabled world.Perhaps the easier competency framework is that of AI competencies. For example, prompt engineering, AI literacy, validation and oversight, ethical and responsible use of AI, agentic AI, and the nature of human-AI collaborations are obvious topics that biomedical education for life sciences research and healthcare delivery must begin to learn. Many programs around the globe have begun offering didactic and practical-based educational programs to serve this need. Perhaps more challenging is the listing of domain-specific competencies. Not every fact that previous generations were expected to memorize will remain equally valuable in an AI-enabled environment. The challenge lies in determining which foundational knowledge remains essential for independent critical thinking and reasoning, and which tasks can appropriately be augmented by AI. Future domain-specific competency frameworks may place less emphasis on memorization and greater emphasis on reasoning, interpretation, critical evaluation, communication, judgement, and collaboration. Each domain needs to develop their list of domain-specific competencies and then design pedagogy, training, and learning assessment around these competencies, assuming that AI will be a partner for the learner. Neither AI competencies nor domain-specific competencies alone are sufficient; future professionals will require mastery of both.The goal should be to leverage AI to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of biomedical research and clinical practice, allowing humans to focus on uniquely human activities such as critical thinking, creativity, and interpersonal connection, rather than repetitive and mundane tasks.Our society has seen workforce transitions before, for example as result of the invention of electricity, the Industrial Revolution, and the emergence of the internet. For example, online streaming services have rendered many jobs unnecessary, such as cashiers in video rental or record stores, while creating thousands of jobs never imagined in the 1990s. Similarly, if the current AI era succeeds some workforce roles will vanish, but many new roles will emerge, some unimaginable today. Leaders, researchers, educators, and workforce members must proactively develop systems and frameworks that enable current and future generations to thrive with AI technology at their fingertips.The future of biomedical research and healthcare should not be defined by "humans in the loop", but by "humans in the lead". Our challenge is not simply to build more capable AI systems. It is to build educational and workforce development frameworks that preserve human expertise while enabling effective human-AI partnership, i.e., systems that are "human-led, AI-enabled." History suggests that AI winters occur when technological capabilities outpace the ability of institutions, professionals, and society to effectively adopt and sustain them. Workforce transformation may therefore be one of the most important safeguards against another cycle of overpromising and underdelivering. If we succeed, AI can become one of the most transformative technologies in the history of medicine. If we fail, another AI winter may be closer than we think.

documents.abstract: This quasi-experimental study investigated the differential effects of human teacher feedback (HTF), AI-generated feedback (AIGF), and hybrid feedback (HF) on learner engagement and argumentative writing quality among 120 undergraduate ESL students across an eight-week intervention. Engagement (behavioural, cognitive, emotional) was measured via a purpose-built questionnaire and revision-tracking logs; writing quality was scored on a five-dimension analytic rubric. Repeated-measures ANOVA and multiple regression showed that HF was associated with the greatest improvement in writing quality (η²p = .24), HTF with the highest proportion of higher-order revisions, and AIGF with the highest revision frequency. Hybrid feedback condition membership was the strongest predictor of writing-quality improvement, followed by cognitive engagement. These findings have implications for AI-integrated writing instruction in higher education.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) contrasts with the limited understanding of its economic, organizational, and societal impacts. This paper develops a conceptual model of Hybrid Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (Hybrid-HCAI), proposing that AI should complement rather than replicate or replace human intelligence. The model integrates three complementary forms of intelligence: subsymbolic AI, symbolic AI, and human intelligence. Subsymbolic AI handles pattern recognition, forecasting, classification, and generation, while symbolic AI represents explicit knowledge, rules, causal relationships, norms, and governance structures. Human intelligence contributes contextual understanding, creativity, intuition, value judgments, social competence, and responsibility. The symbolic layer additionally mediates and regulates interactions between human and machine intelligence, functioning as a “social operating system” for coordination. The paper derives a theoretical impact model focusing on productivity, organizational agility, innovation, structural stability, and cultural integrity. Participation, reciprocity, fairness, trust, and recognition of cognitive contributions serve as key mediators and design variables. The study proposes empirically testable hypotheses and an interdisciplinary research agenda, positioning Hybrid-HCAI as a conceptual research program rather than a validated technology.

documents.abstract: This conference presentation examines the multifaceted impact of artificial intelligence (AI) proliferation on internet security, cybersecurity practices, software engineering, and digital sovereignty. It considers both the defensive capabilities enabled by AI technologies and the emerging security risks associated with their widespread adoption. The presentation discusses how AI-based solutions can improve cyberattack detection, threat analysis, incident response, and vulnerability identification. At the same time, it highlights the growing potential for malicious applications, including automated malware generation, phishing, deepfakes, social engineering, and disinformation. Particular attention is devoted to security vulnerabilities in AI-driven and agentic systems, including prompt injection, jailbreaking, training data poisoning, goal hijacking, and context manipulation. The analysis addresses the risks associated with excessive system privileges, persistent access to external tools, non-deterministic behavior, and dependencies on untrusted information sources. Security mitigation approaches include static and dynamic application security testing, the principle of least privilege, zero-trust architectures, sandboxed execution, and input/output validation. The presentation also explores the implications of AI-assisted software development, emphasizing the necessity of comprehensive code review, testing, and validation. It identifies potential challenges associated with vibe coding, cognitive debt, declining opportunities for junior developers, and the erosion of organizational knowledge and technical expertise. Broader societal and regulatory considerations include digital sovereignty, technological dependencies, open-source alternatives, responsible AI governance, and emerging European initiatives supporting technological autonomy. The presentation concludes that artificial intelligence can become a strategic asset for cybersecurity when AI models are developed using high-quality data, deployed within appropriate security frameworks, and subjected to effective human oversight and governance.

Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. Furthermore, building upon the comprehensive findings from our computational experiments, we propose flexible, parameterizable data privacy practice designs based on the notion of revelation protection. The proposed approach is designed to provide an effective balance between personalization performance and privacy considerations, as demonstrated using extensive simulation experiments. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of privacy-aware recommender systems in the context of contemporary data protection regulations. The findings can also be informative to policymakers for understanding the practical implications of various data privacy practices and for designing future policies.

Continuous design for quality and safety in healthcare and implementation science are fundamentally connected fields with a shared mission: systematically and sustainably improving healthcare and outcomes. Panel discussions at the 2025 HFES Healthcare Symposium and ASPIRE Annual Meeting explored how these fields can strengthen each other in practice. This work synthesizes lessons learned from these discussions and research developments at the nexus of these fields, laying groundwork for an integrative research agenda.

Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within Italian educational contexts represents one of the most complex digital transitions of the contemporary world (Han et al., 2022; Hopcan et al., 2023). Following the pandemic experience and the lockdown, schools have witnessed a proliferation of training offers for teachers, both curricular and specialized in support, often characterized by huge efforts. In this scenario, AI cannot be reduced to a simple instrumental innovation; in fact, it requires a profound redefinition of educational design and professional roles. Abandoning an initial technooptimism, international research today requires a critical-reflective approach: integrating these technologies without analyzing their ethical assumptions risks amplifying existing inequalities. As a result, the distinction proposed in the literature between an AI used "instead of education", which replaces the relationship, and an AI used "for education", which acts in support of human pedagogical goals, becomes fundamental (Holmes et al., 2022). documents.abstract: ABSTRACT: This study investigated the influence of artificial intelligence and learning analytics on the performance of postgraduate students in universities in Cross River State, Nigeria. The study specifically examined the influence of artificial intelligence technologies, ethical implications of artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and ethical implications of learning analytics on postgraduate students’ learning. Four research questions and four null hypotheses guided the study. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study was conducted in public universities offering postgraduate programmes in Cross River State. A sample of 300 postgraduate students was selected using a multistage sampling technique involving purposive, stratified random, and proportionate sampling procedures. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled *Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics Influence Questionnaire (AILAIQ)*. The instrument was validated by three experts in Educational Technology and Measurement and Evaluation, while a reliability coefficient of 0.84 was obtained using Cronbach’s Alpha. Data collected were analyzed using simple linear regression to answer the research questions, while regression t-test was used to test the null hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that artificial intelligence technologies had a significant positive influence on postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 6.7% of the variance in learning outcomes (R = .259, R² = .067, t = 5.132, p < .05). Ethical implications of artificial intelligence also had a significant influence, accounting for 13.3% of the variance (R = .365, R² = .133, t = 7.512, p < .05). Learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, although its contribution was relatively small, accounting for 1.2% of the variance (R = .109, R² = .012, t = 2.107, p = .036). Similarly, ethical implications of learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 7.9% of the variance (R = .282, R² = .079, t = 5.627, p < .05). Based on these findings, the study concluded that artificial intelligence and learning analytics, as well as the ethical conditions surrounding their use, significantly influence postgraduate students’ learning in universities in Cross River State. The study recommended, among others, that universities should strategically integrate AI and learning analytics into postgraduate education, develop clear ethical frameworks for their use, strengthen digital infrastructure, and provide adequate training for lecturers and students on the responsible and effective use of these technologies. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, learning analytics, ethical implications, postgraduate students, academic performance, universities, Cross River State.

Background Deep tabular models, including self-supervised and pretrained foundation models, are increasingly proposed for clinical risk prediction, but their value over conventional learners is rarely tested against matched controls, and their role relative to clinician judgement is seldom examined. Methods In a retrospective single-centre cohort of 879 women referred for colposcopy (242 CIN2+, 27.5%), 15 routinely recorded variables, including a clinician image-based assessment documented before histopathology, were modelled with ten model families under one fixed protocol (single fold assignment and seed, no tuning). Discrimination was compared by paired DeLong tests and bootstrap. Two analyses were pre-specified: exact Shapley attribution of discrimination to five clinical groups of variables in every model family, and a complementarity analysis asking whether routine data identify CIN2+ among women judged negative by the clinician. Frozen models were evaluated in a 103-case two-centre external cohort. Results Out-of-fold AUROC ranged from 0.726 to 0.761. No model outperformed logistic regression (AUROC 0.757; CatBoost −0.002, p = 0.860; TabPFN +0.004, p = 0.554), and three matched ablations of a self-supervised tabular Transformer were null (all p ≥ 0.096). Removing the clinician assessment lowered AUROC in all ten families (by 0.041 to 0.072; all p ≤ 0.008). Shapley attribution ranked five variable groups identically in every family (Kendall’s W = 1.00; permutation p < 0.001): the clinician assessment (39% to 50% of discrimination above chance), then cytology, HPV testing, colposcopic findings and demographic history. The clinician assessment alone had sensitivity 0.504 and specificity 0.882; 49.6% of CIN2+ occurred in clinician-negative women. Re-reviewing the 20% of clinician-negative women with the highest model risk identified 34.2% (95% CI 25.7–42.7%) of the missed CIN2+, against 20% expected at random, raising pathway sensitivity to 0.674 at specificity 0.733. External AUROC of logistic regression was 0.710. Conclusions On routine structured data from a colposcopy-referral population, and under a common protocol, model architecture did not determine performance; predictor information did. Retrospectively, routine data complemented the clinician modestly in clinician-negative women, rather than replacing clinical judgement. Claims that complex architectures improve clinical tabular prediction should be tested against logistic regression with paired uncertainty across repeated data splits.

In the age of the Fourth Revolution, understood not only as the convergence of cyber -physical systems and artificial intelligence but also as a mutation of human self-understanding, the sharp distinction between online and offline dissolves into a constitutively hybrid "onlife" condition. Digital environments do not merely transmit information: they orchestrate emotional states, modulate attention and construct reputational identities, acting upon a subjectivity solicited from within rather than repressed from without. Setting out from Asimov's short story Evidence and the figure of the "maimed master", the essay locates the true terrain of the educational challenge not in computational power but in empathy and affectivity. The risk is not that machines will become human, but that humanity will grow accustomed to a synthetic affectivity, devoid of the weight of the body and of the responsibility inherent in relationship. Abstract Education is undergoing a significant transformation in response to technological development, changing social conditions, emerging employment opportunities and the increasing demand for practical and skill-oriented learning. In this context, innovation in education has become an important area of discussion in India. Educational innovation, however, should not be understood merely as the introduction of computers, smart classrooms or artificial intelligence. It includes changes in teaching methods, curriculum, assessment, classroom interaction, institutional practices and the relationship between education and society. The present paper examines the changing nature of educational innovation in India with particular reference to school and higher education. It analyses India's policy direction under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and discusses initiatives such as PM SHRI Schools, Atal Tinkering Labs, Frontier Technology Labs, digital education platforms, experiential learning and technology-enabled higher education. The paper also examines evidence from UDISE+ and the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 to understand the realities of educational development, particularly in rural India. ASER 2024 provides evidence on enrolment, foundational learning and, for the first time at national scale, digital access, usage and skills among children aged 14–16. The paper argues that India's emerging model of educational innovation is gradually moving from a technology-centred approach towards a broader model involving experiential learning, creativity, problem-solving, digital literacy, vocational exposure, holistic assessment and community participation. At the same time, challenges such as the digital divide, infrastructure limitations, teacher preparedness, unequal access and the tension between innovative pedagogy and conventional assessment continue to affect implementation. The study concludes that educational innovation becomes meaningful only when technology, teachers, students, curriculum and local context work together to improve actual learning.

In many work environments, professionals perform physically demanding routines involving repetitive movements and prolonged static postures, increasing exposure to biomechanical risk factors associated with work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs). Wearable technologies offer opportunities for continuous posture monitoring and real-time feedback, but their occupational deployment remains challenging due to limitations related to comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and integration with work clothing. This scoping review aims to synthesize and critically analyze the existing evidence on smart-textile-based wearable systems for occupational posture monitoring. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and CINAHL was conducted, identifying 566 records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 34 studies were included in the final synthesis. The included studies were analyzed according to wearable architectures, sensing technologies, data processing and posture recognition, user feedback mechanisms, and energy management strategies. Hybrid architectures combining textile-based sensors and inertial measurement units, together with machine learning and real-time feedback, emerged as promising approaches for continuous posture monitoring. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical or laboratory validation, with relatively small samples and limited long-term evaluation in real occupational environments. Five studies reported changes in posture or ergonomic behavior following the use of the technology, while no direct evidence of reductions in WRMSD incidence or severity was identified. Overall, the findings demonstrate substantial technological potential for smart-textile-based posture monitoring, but current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical or occupational effectiveness in preventing WRMSDs. Future research should prioritize prospective, long-term validation involving larger and more diverse worker populations under real-world occupational conditions, while addressing comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and compatibility with occupational clothing and personal protective equipment.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence within educational environments is profoundly reshaping language teaching. Language teachers are increasingly expected to operate in digitally mediated environments and to integrate technological tools into their pedagogical practice (Godwin-Jones, 2022). Yet resistance remains widespread. Without adequate training that addresses both the technical and pedagogical dimensions of AI use, hesitation is a predictable and, in many respects, rational response. The literature confirms that resistance to AI adoption stems from a structural deficit: limited preparation, insufficient theoretical grounding, and the absence of models that connect technological tools to principled language pedagogy (Godwin-Jones, 2022; Kovačić & Bubaš, 2023). This challenge is particularly acute in LSP education, where language learning is inseparable from disciplinary discourse, professional communication, and context-sensitive language use. Specialized discourse cannot be reduced to automated linguistic processing, and teachers who lack a robust pedagogical framework struggle to evaluate what AI tools can and cannot do within their specific instructional contexts. Abstract Rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities worldwide to issue guidelines on student AI use in assessment. While existing research catalogues policy content and student misuse, little is known about how students perceive these guidelines and how such perceptions shape behaviour. This paper argues that current research treats guidelines as a binary intervention—present or absent—overlooking their psychological and institutional authenticity. Drawing on procedural justice and neutralisation theories, we contend that when guidelines are vague, invisible, unenforceable, and treated by academics as box-ticking exercises, they fail as integrity safeguards and may instead provide justifications for disingenuous AI use. We further argue that this pattern reflects institutional compulsions—legal, reputational, and competitive—that drive guideline issuance despite known limitations. We propose a research agenda centred on guideline authenticity and its effects on fairness perceptions, moral neutralisation, and compliance intentions, alongside perceptions of institutional motivation. A sequential mixed-methods design is outlined, drawing on UAE and UK contexts. The agenda aims to move institutional practice beyond symbolic policy-making toward genuinely embedded academic integrity cultures.

The growing use of artificial intelligence in education raises questions about how emotional experience, relational care, and professional responsibility can be sustained in increasingly data-mediated teaching environments. This conceptual article examines instructional emotion as an interrelated configuration of teachers’ emotional engagement, students’ learning-related experiences, and the affective relationships through which teaching acquires meaning. Drawing on scholarship on achievement emotions, caring pedagogy, teacher–student relationships, and artificial intelligence in education, the article organizes its analysis around three value foundations: embodied human experience, relational connection, and teachers’ professional responsibility. It then identifies four potential forms of alienation arising when technological efficiency overrides educational judgment: procedural rigidity in teaching methods, emotional distance in interaction, the loss of affective meaning in content, and the reduction of assessment to measurable performance. Corresponding reconstruction pathways include emotionally adaptive instructional design, humanistic interaction, affective knowledge graphs, and emotionally responsive assessment. These pathways are guided by teacher judgment and bounded by consent, fairness, transparency, and human oversight. The framework distinguishes the interpretation of emotional evidence from claims to measure learners’ inner states directly. Its contribution is to connect educational values, potential risks, and pedagogical responses within a coherent conceptual structure. The proposed relationships remain open to empirical examination across educational settings.

Oman’s digitisation priorities under Oman Vision 2040 encourage the integration of technology into teaching and learning. Little research examines instructors’ perceptions of Microsoft Teams (MS Teams) Reading Progress in Omani General Foundation Programme (GFP) contexts, particularly regarding its pedagogical value, ease of use, and implementation challenges. This mixed-methods pilot study explored instructors’ perceptions of Reading Progress in General English 2 (GE2), within the pre-degree GFP at the Preparatory Studies Centre (PSC), University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS), Oman. MS Teams Reading Progress is an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported tool designed to help students practice reading aloud, improve accuracy and fluency, and give instructors performance data. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this study explored instructors’ perceptions of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions, and behavioural intention. Using purposive sampling, data were collected from three sources: a structured questionnaire (N = 10), two semi-structured interviews, and MS Teams usage logs. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed thematically. The findings reveal a disconnect between teachers’ positive perceptions and willingness to continue using the tool and students’ limited engagement. Although instructors believed the tool could support reading fluency and accuracy, its use remained low, possibly due to the timing of the pilot, the absence of continuous assessment (CA), and limited time within the course plan. The findings indicate that wider implementation would benefit from early rollout, integration into course design, and CA weighting.

Abstract The conventional Charpy impact test provides a single primary measure of material performance: the total energy absorbed during fracture. When strain gauges or piezoelectric sensors are incorporated into the striker, however, the test can record force as a function of time and displacement throughout the impact. These measurements provide a more detailed picture of how a material responds and fractures under dynamic loading. The conventional Charpy impact test provides a single primary measure of material performance: the total energy absorbed during fracture. However, by incorporating strain gauges or piezoelectric sensors into the striker, the test can provide continuous force-time and force-displacement data throughout the fracture event, offering substantially more detailed information on the material’s dynamic fracture behavior. This review traces the development of the instrumented Charpy impact test from its early twentieth-century origins to its current applications. The fundamental principles underlying the measurement are described, with particular emphasis on the characteristic forces identified from the force-displacement curve and their physical significance. The final section of this review considers emerging works that may push instrumented Charpy testing further. Among the most promising directions are machine learning and artificial intelligence, digital twin technology, robotic automation, and high-speed digital image correlation (DIC).

ABSTRACT Marine surveyors are routinely exposed to complex hazards, chemical, ergonomic, and physical, within dynamic environments such as ships and offshore platforms. Existing personal protective equipment (PPE) provides only basic safeguards and remains largely reactive. This paper proposes the design and conceptual architecture of an AI‐enhanced smart PPE boiler suit specifically optimized for marine and offshore class surveyors. The proposed system is envisioned to leverage embedded sensor networks, edge/cloud artificial intelligence analytics, and real‐time communications for continuous hazard detection, predictive risk mitigation, and streamlined survey workflows. We detail a proposed system architecture, outline pathways for functional prototyping, and critically examine anticipated challenges, establishing a robust roadmap for future multidisciplinary research and industry adoption. No physical prototype has been constructed at this stage; all scenarios and performance figures presented herein are theoretical and intended to guide future empirical validation.

We wrap up the discussion with a reflection on techniques how to interact with stakeholders. Within scientific software development, stakeholders involve intra- and extra-institutional colleagues on different career levels, maturity and with different intrinsic motivation. There certainly are further groups such as the general public or businesses. The present chapter narrows the discussion down to academic collaborators for which we discuss interaction techniques as opposed to scheduling from Section 14.8 . Even within this narrow focus, the list of techniques refrains from an attempt to exhaustively map and discuss the different stakeholder groups. Instead, some common communication techniques that have proven valuable are distilled, and the focus falls exclusively on interaction patterns as they affect day-to-day development work. The developer's point of view is prioritised.

This white paper is the deliverable of work package 2.5 “Interdisciplinary evaluation protocols” (german: “Interdisziplinäre Evaluierungsprotokolle”) of the Center for Assistive Technologies Rhein-Ruhr (Zentrum Assistive Technologien Rhein-Ruhr, ZAT, see Wild-Wall et al. 2024). It addresses the evaluation of assistive technology (AT), which we define as any device, software, equipment, or system that enables people with disabilities, functional limitations or special needs to perform specific tasks. The purpose of evaluating AT is to assess, in a systematic and reproducible manner, how effectively it fulfills its intended function in close interplay with the human user(s). Because AT, by definition, interacts with people, its evaluation must account not only for technological performance but also for social and human factors. A meaningful and comprehensive evaluation therefore requires an interdisciplinary perspective, drawing on the methodological toolkits of multiple disciplines and approaches.

documents.abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.

Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

ABSTRACT Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) are a major occupational health problem in the informal sector, particularly among traditional weavers who work in repetitive postures for extended periods. Traditional ikat weavers in Fatubenao Village, Atambua City, Belu Regency, experience significant musculoskeletal complaints due to prolonged awkward postures. This study aimed to analyze the effect of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in reducing musculoskeletal disorder complaints among traditional ikat weavers. A quasi-experimental study with a non-equivalent control group design was conducted on 30 respondents (15 intervention, 15 control). MSDs complaints were measured using the Nordic Body Map (NBM) instrument covering 28 body regions. Omega-3 supplementation was administered for 14 days. Data analysis used the Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test and Mann-Whitney Test. The highest MSDs complaints prior to intervention were found in left and right ankle (76.7%), lower back (73.3%), left wrist (70.0%), and left upper arm (63.3%). Wilcoxon test showed significant reduction in the intervention group (Z = -3.417; p = 0.001). Mann-Whitney posttest revealed a significant difference between intervention and control groups (U = 54.000; p = 0.014). Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for 14 days significantly reduced MSDs complaints among traditional ikat weavers. This non-pharmacological intervention is safe, affordable, and effective for controlling MSDs in informal sector workers. Keywords: Omega-3 Supplementation, Musculoskeletal Disorders, Traditional Weavers, Nordic Body Map, Occupational Health. ABSTRAK Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) merupakan masalah kesehatan kerja utama di sektor informal, khususnya pada penenun ikat tradisional yang bekerja dalam postur berulang dalam durasi lama. Penenun ikat tradisional di Kelurahan Fatubenao, Kecamatan Kota Atambua, Kabupaten Belu mengalami keluhan muskuloskeletal yang signifikan akibat postur kerja tidak ergonomis yang berkepanjangan. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis efektivitas suplementasi asam lemak omega-3 dalam menurunkan keluhan Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) pada penenun ikat tradisional. Studi kuasi-eksperimental dengan desain non-equivalent control group dilakukan pada 30 responden (15 kelompok perlakuan, 15 kelompok kontrol). Keluhan MSDs diukur menggunakan instrumen Nordic Body Map (NBM) mencakup 28 area tubuh. Suplemen omega-3 diberikan selama 14 hari. Analisis data menggunakan Uji Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test dan Mann-Whitney Test. Keluhan MSDs tertinggi sebelum intervensi ditemukan pada pergelangan kaki kiri dan kanan (76,7%), punggung bawah (73,3%), pergelangan tangan kiri (70,0%), dan lengan atas kiri (63,3%). Uji Wilcoxon menunjukkan penurunan signifikan pada kelompok perlakuan (Z = -3,417; p = 0,001). Uji Mann-Whitney posttest menunjukkan perbedaan bermakna antara kelompok perlakuan dan kontrol (U = 54,000; p = 0,014). Suplementasi asam lemak omega-3 selama 14 hari secara signifikan menurunkan keluhan MSDs pada penenun ikat tradisional. Intervensi non-farmakologis ini aman, terjangkau, dan efektif untuk pengendalian MSDs pada pekerja sektor informal. Kata Kunci: Suplementasi Omega-3, Muskuloskeletal Disorders, Penenun Tradisional, Nordic Body Map, Kesehatan Kerja.

documents.abstract: This work presents a systematic review on self-management, leisure, youth and wellbeing, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Considering the long research tradition in leisure studies addressing youth wellbeing but the scarce evidence available on leisure-based interventions specifically promoting self-management and its favourable influences on non-vulnerable and vulnerable youth, the following research question was answered through this systematic review: what interventions or good practices in self-management of leisure have an impact on wellbeing among youth, both vulnerable and non-vulnerable youth? After applying the PRISMA 2020 protocol, several studies with strong relevance to the topic of study were reviewed, and the main findings were discussed. The discussion covers key topics addressed in the reviewed literature regarding self-management, leisure, youth and wellbeing outcomes, as well as features or types of interventions working on self-management with a greater contribution to youth wellbeing. In this regard, interventions satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness consistently yield higher intrinsic motivation and wellbeing; youth who independently organise leisure report higher satisfaction and emotional benefits; and team-based interventions outperform individual or sedentary pursuits in perceived wellbeing. Moreover, important gaps in the literature were identified so that future research can be oriented towards closing them, such as the age bias with a predominant focus on ages from 10 to 19 years, which leaves emerging adults (20–29) underrepresented; the short-term focus due to most studies measuring only pre-to-post outcomes instead of long-term impact with scarce follow-up data; and geographical and cultural gaps, as the literature is concentrated in Western cultures.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has introduced complex ethical challenges that require critical examination through religious and moral perspectives, including Islamic ethics. This study aims to systematically map the intellectual structure, research development, collaborative networks, and emerging thematic trends in scholarly literature concerning Islamic ethics in the digital era. Employing a bibliometric approach, the study utilizes VOSviewer to conduct citation analysis, co-authorship analysis, institutional and country collaboration mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, overlay visualization, and density visualization. The findings reveal that Islamic digital ethics constitutes an increasingly interdisciplinary research domain encompassing artificial intelligence, digital communication, Islamic finance, blockchain, and sustainable digital transformation. Citation analysis identifies blockchain, financial technology, and Islamic finance as influential areas of scholarly contribution. The collaboration analysis demonstrates the prominent roles of Indonesia and Malaysia in international research networks, although institutional collaboration remains relatively concentrated. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies artificial intelligence, Islamic ethics, digital ethics, social media, and ethical principles as dominant themes. Furthermore, overlay visualization indicates a thematic transition from digital financial applications and communication technologies toward machine learning, digital transformation, and sustainable development. Density visualization confirms the concentration of scholarly attention around artificial intelligence and ethical frameworks while revealing comparatively less developed thematic areas. The study highlights the importance of integrating Islamic ethical principles, particularly trustworthiness, justice, accountability, and public welfare, into contemporary technological governance. These findings contribute to the literature by providing a systematic understanding of the field's intellectual landscape and identifying potential directions for future interdisciplinary research on responsible artificial intelligence, data privacy, algorithmic accountability, and sustainable digital innovation.

This part examines Eric Miller’s contribution to the development and application of socio-technical systems (STS) theory within the Tavistock Institute tradition. Building on foundational studies of British coal mining by Trist and Bamforth, Miller advanced the understanding that organizations comprise interdependent social and technical systems whose misalignment produces inefficiency, low morale, and resistance to change. He argued that effective organizational design depends on recognizing organizations as open systems embedded in dynamic environments and on addressing human, structural, and technological factors simultaneously. Central to Miller’s approach was the principle of joint optimization, which holds that neither technical efficiency nor social well-being can be prioritized in isolation. He emphasized participative work design, advocating the involvement of employees in shaping new technologies and processes so that work systems support task performance, autonomy, and collaboration. This perspective informed his support for autonomous and semi-autonomous work groups, demonstrating that responsibility, discretion, and meaningful roles enhance motivation, learning, and innovation. Miller also stressed adaptability and environmental fit, arguing that resilient organizations require flexible structures capable of responding to technological, economic, and social change. As a consultant, he applied STS through action research, positioning the consultant as a facilitator of organizational learning rather than a technical expert. His legacy endures in contemporary organizational practices, such as agile methods, self-managing teams, and human-centred design, where balancing system performance with human experience remains a central challenge.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the university landscape offers unprecedented efficiency and speed, radically transforming how students access information and fulfill their academic responsibilities. However, this instantaneous convenience gives rise to a critical shift: do contemporary students remain autonomous knowledge producers, or have they been reduced to mere curators who synthesize and rearrange content from digital repositories? This paper critically examines the dynamics of student learning and assignment completion amidst the expanding AI ecosystem. Employing a reflective-critical approach, the article highlights the paradox of digital efficiency—which accelerates academic processes on one hand, yet risks diminishing critical depth, intellectual autonomy, and student creativity on the other. The analysis reveals that the relationship between students and AI is not merely instrumental; rather, it actively reshapes structural study habits, demanding a profound pedagogical redefinition to ensure that university institutions preserve the fundamental essence of knowledge creation.
