documents.abstract: Background: Manual scavenging continues to expose workers to serious chemical, physical, and biological hazards despite legal restrictions in India. These risks are intensified by poor protective practices and limited occupational health support. Aim was to assess occupational health hazards, knowledge, and preventive practices among manual scavengers and to examine their association with selected demographic variables. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 100 manual scavengers in Kanpur using purposive sampling. Data were collected through a structured interview schedule including self-reported occupational health hazards assessment, knowledge, and preventive practices. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation, and chi-square test. Results: Chemical, physical, and biological hazards were commonly reported. Moderate knowledge was found in 61% of participants with mean knowledge score of 15.1±3.21, while poor preventive practices were observed in 49%. Biological hazards showed a significant negative correlation with knowledge (r=−0.201, p=0.044) while knowledge and preventive practices were significantly associated with age, education, type of work, work experience, family size, and gender. Conclusions: Manual scavengers in Kanpur experience substantial occupational risk with inadequate preventive practices. Targeted occupational health education, provision of protective equipment, and policy-level support are urgently needed.

documents.abstract: The spread of digital technologies and artificial intelligence is profoundly transforming educational processes, necessitating a shift away from an exclusively technocentric view of innovation. As Selwyn (2016) and Floridi (2014) highlight, technologies are not mere tools, but environments that influence the construction of knowledge, relationships, and professional identities. The literature highlights how emotions, trust, and a sense of belonging significantly influence participation in digital environments ( Zembylas ,2015). From this perspective, social presence (Garrison, Anderson, & Archer, 2000) and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999) become important. This paper analyses the role of an open digital space in building an emotionally aware learning environment within the specialisation courses for support activities (TFA). The research adopts a qualitative action research approach supported by descriptive quantitative data. The study involved 1,500 students enrolled in TFA programs from different Italian regions. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 177-178. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.

Healthcare organizations are enabling AI-embedded ERP features faster than governance rules are being written for them, and in mid-2026 the rules arrived faster than most solution architects expected. The Coalition for Health AI published eight governance playbooks on 27 May 2026, and five days later the Joint Commission opened its voluntary Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare certification, which means a surveyor can now ask a health system to demonstrate its AI governance rather than describe it. Neither document specifies which system setting enforces any of it, and arguably neither should, since both are written to apply across every vendor a health system might run. This paper closes that gap for one platform. Six governance domains running through the CHAI playbooks and RUAIH guidance, namely accountability, transparency, human oversight, pre-deployment risk assessment, continuous monitoring, and third-party risk, are each mapped to a control that already exists inside Oracle Cloud ERP: role-based security profiles, approval hierarchies, and the execution traceability introduced with Oracle's 2026 Fusion Agentic Applications and AI Agent Studio. The mapping is supported by a four-tier risk model that determines how much autonomy an agent may hold, an audit evidence model stating what a surveyor should be shown for each domain, and a six-step implementation sequence. The contribution is a practitioner synthesis drawn from Oracle Cloud ERP transformation programs in regulated health systems. It is not a controlled study, and no compliance outcome, audit finding rate, or certification result is reported or claimed.

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce platforms has resulted in a large volume of customer-generated product reviews. These reviews contain valuable information about customer opinions, satisfaction levels, product quality, and specific product features. However, manually analysing a large number of reviews is time-consuming and difficult. Opinion mining, also known as sentiment analysis, uses Artificial Intelligence and Natural Language Processing techniques to automatically identify and classify opinions expressed in textual reviews. This paper presents a conceptual AI-based framework for analysing product reviews and identifying their sentiment polarity as positive, negative, or neutral. The proposed approach combines contextual language representation using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) with aspect-based sentiment analysis inspired by Aspect-specific Graph Convolutional Networks (ASGCN). The system performs review preprocessing, contextual feature extraction, aspect identification, sentiment classification, and generation of an overall opinion summary. The reviewed literature also includes hybrid BERT-CNN architectures, user/context-aware graph modelling, and multimodal learning approaches, which provide additional directions for improving opinion analysis. The proposed framework aims to provide more detailed and meaningful information than simple positive or negative classification by identifying the product aspects responsible for customer opinions. Such a system can assist customers in decision-making and help businesses understand product strengths, weaknesses, and areas requiring improvement

This contribution presents an exploratory study on pre-service teachers' perceptions of the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in lesson planning, with a focus on opportunities, risks, and conditions for effective integration into instructional design. The study is grounded in the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) and its extension Intelligent-TPACK (Celik, 2023), which incorporates an explicit ethical dimension into teachers' technological and pedagogical knowledge. Within this perspective, AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, and automated planning systems are not neutral instruments but sociotechnical systems that require critical evaluation in terms of transparency, fairness, and accountability. The theoretical approach adopted here is further informed by critical AI literacy perspectives, which emphasise the need for teachers to develop not only operational competence but also the ability to interrogate the assumptions and biases embedded in algorithmic outputs. documents.abstract: This study aims to examine the effectiveness of the Arabic language tutoring program (bimbingan belajar Bahasa Arab) at SMK Negeri 1 Mesuji, Ogan Komering Ilir Regency, where the dropout rate reaches 17.3%, and to formulate an optimization model for that program grounded in Pendidikan Akidah Akhlak (Islamic Creed and Morals Education) to build students' character and resilience and to prevent dropout. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study used primary data from students, teachers, and parents. Of the students actively participating in the Arabic language tutoring program, 50 respondents were selected through stratified random sampling (Slovin formula) to complete a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire, which was analyzed using multiple linear regression in SPSS 26. Qualitative data were collected through in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and participant observation with key informants selected through purposive sampling, and were analyzed thematically using NVivo 12. Quantitative results show that the effectiveness of the Arabic language tutoring was mostly in the moderate category (76%) and did not significantly affect Akidah Akhlak-based resilience (t = 0.340; sig = 0.735), whereas intrinsic motivation did (t = 2.587; sig = 0.013; R² = 0.400). Qualitative findings show that informants regard the Arabic tutoring as helpful for understanding the material yet still academically oriented, that spiritual resilience is students' primary coping mechanism against external constraints, and that all informants expect an Arabic language tutoring model that integrates Akidah Akhlak. The study proposes an optimization model for Arabic language tutoring built on five strategies: integrating Akidah Akhlak values into Arabic tutoring materials, strengthening intrinsic motivation and character, adopting a holistic learning approach, fostering school–teacher–parent collaboration, and providing continuous mentoring for students at risk of dropping out.

The rapid acceleration of digital transformation has changed the way organizations formulate and implement business strategies, requiring firms to become more adaptive, data-driven, and responsive to dynamic market conditions. This study aims to examine how big data and artificial intelligence can be orchestrated as integrated strategic capabilities to support adaptive digital business strategy. Using a qualitative conceptual approach, this study applies a structured literature review and thematic synthesis to analyze previous studies related to big data capability, artificial intelligence capability, governance mechanisms, intelligent business insight, and strategic adaptability. The results show that big data functions as a strategic foundation by providing diverse information from customers, markets, operations, and digital platforms, while artificial intelligence acts as an intelligent decision engine that transforms data into predictions, recommendations, automation, and actionable business insights. The findings also indicate that governance and human decision-making are essential in ensuring that the use of big data and AI remains reliable, transparent, accountable, secure, and aligned with organizational objectives. This study concludes that adaptive digital business strategy emerges from the continuous orchestration of data resources, AI systems, governance structures, human judgment, and strategic execution. The proposed framework contributes to digital business literature by explaining how AI-driven big data orchestration can improve decision quality, agility, competitiveness, innovation, operational efficiency, and sustainable digital value creation. In addition, the discussion is expanded to include cybersecurity, data privacy, secure data processing, and AI risk management as critical enablers of large-scale data-driven business systems.

This chapter provides an overview of Eric Miller’s contribution to organizational development and industrial democracy, situating his practice within the Tavistock tradition that integrates open systems thinking, socio-technical systems (STS) design, and psychoanalytic perspectives on group and organizational life. Miller argued that organizations are not merely rational structures, but emotional and social systems in which anxiety, defence, and unconscious processes shape behaviour, decision-making, and capacity for change. Central to his approach is the concept of the organization as an open system whose viability depends on effective boundary management, between sub-systems, levels of authority, and the organization and its environment. Building on STS principles, Miller emphasized joint optimization: designing technical processes and social arrangements in tandem so that task requirements and human needs are aligned. He extended this work by making visible the defensive patterns that emerge under stress, splitting, projection, denial, scapegoating, and rigidity, and by showing how authority and leadership often become focal points for organizational anxieties. His consultancy therefore combined structural diagnosis with reflective inquiry into role, power, and emotional experience. The chapter illustrates these themes through emblematic cases: the coal mining studies that shaped STS foundations; applications in healthcare where hierarchy and communication can become defensive; work with the Church of England on identity and authority in a changing environment; and the Norwegian Industrial Democracy Project, demonstrating how participative work design can enhance resilience and performance. Overall, this part frames Miller’s legacy as a disciplined, practice-oriented synthesis of system and psyche, offering enduring concepts for contemporary organizational change.

Introduction Digital public health transformation extends beyond technology deployment and requires organizational processes that align interpretation, coordination, governance, and population-health goals. Existing research examines change communication, collective sensemaking, and cross-functional collaboration separately, with limited integration of their boundaries, recursive interactions, cross-level transmission, and multilevel outcomes. This review develops an organizational explanation of how these mechanisms may support transformation. Methods A narrative integrative review synthesized theoretical, empirical, policy, and technical literature from organizational science, implementation science, digital public health, data governance, and artificial intelligence governance. Searches covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, APA PsycINFO, CINAHL, IEEE Xplore, ProQuest Public Health Database, Business Source Complete, and traceable institutional sources from inception to October 1, 2026. Sources were purposively selected for relevance, contribution, public health applicability, analytical level, and traceability. Synthesis used construct coding, within-theme comparison, framework comparison, cross-level mechanism mapping, and analysis of competing explanations and evidence boundaries. Results Change communication establishes credible and contestable direction; collective sensemaking develops shared problem representations; cross-functional collaboration translates shared understanding into coordinated action. They operate recursively rather than sequentially. A seven-layer framework links structural contextual conditions, organizational mechanisms, potential mediating capabilities, implementation outcomes, organizational or system outcomes, population-level service and equity outcomes, and population health outcomes. Team psychological safety moderates the relationship between proximal support conditions and risk-detection behaviors, which feed back into the mechanisms. Organizational readiness for change, knowledge absorption and translation, interoperability governance, organizational learning, and resilience are proposed as mediating capabilities. Power and equity governance, community decision rights, representativeness, vendor accountability, auditing, appeals, portability, and exit management cut across the framework. The model complements CFIR, NASSS, i-PARIHS, EPIS, and sociotechnical approaches by specifying observable interactive mechanisms and feedback pathways. Discussion The framework provides a testable explanatory structure and governance-diagnostic tool for surveillance, data infrastructures, laboratory networks, artificial intelligence, and community co-production. Evidence more strongly supports organizational and system processes than causal effects on population health. Longitudinal, multilevel, and mechanism-oriented studies should test mediation, moderation, feedback, equity, and cross-level transmission.

The rapid adoption of generative AI (GenAI) among university students has raised concerns that excessive trust in AI outputs may erode critical thinking. This study examines how overtrust relates to critical thinking through cognitive offloading and AI dependency, with AI literacy as a protective moderator, integrating partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with machine learning. Survey data from 580 Vietnamese undergraduates were analysed through a five-step pipeline: exploratory structure learning, confirmatory path estimation, predictive benchmarking, explainable AI, and heterogeneous-effect estimation. Overtrust was associated with higher offloading (β = 0.390) and dependency (β = 0.402), both of which were associated with lower critical thinking (β = -0.251 and -0.348), while AI literacy buffered the association with dependency (interaction β = 0.154). Crucially, the direct effect of overtrust was non-significant and the two mediators carried 89% of its total effect, indicating indirect-only mediation. A parsimonious six-variable classifier separated at-risk students with AUC ≈ 0.77, whereas demographics alone performed at chance; SHAP analysis identified AI dependency as the dominant feature in the classification decision, and a causal forest confirmed the buffering pattern across the low-to-mid range while exposing a non-monotonic reversal under sparse support at the upper tail. Interventions should therefore target AI-use behaviour rather than trust itself. These findings are associational rather than causal: the design is cross-sectional with all measures self-reported at a single point, so the classifier performs concurrent screening rather than temporal prediction.

The contemporary global educational landscape is increasingly vulnerable to systemic crises, including natural disasters, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, and socioeconomic instability. These events do not merely interrupt educational continuity; they exacerbate existing social, economic, and geographic inequalities, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations (Burde et al., 2017). In this context, Education in Emergencies (EiE) must be understood not only as a temporary humanitarian response, but as a structural and pedagogical imperative for safeguarding the universal right to education. Educational resilience therefore requires a shift from reactive and fragmented models toward proactive and adaptive systems capable of anticipating, absorbing, and recovering from crises without compromising the quality and equity of teaching and learning. This resilience cannot be achieved without integrating the psychological, emotional, and relational dimensions of education. Trauma-informed education highlights how large-scale crises can profoundly affect students, families, and teachers, altering stress regulation and compromising cognitive, executive, and socio-relational functioning essential to learning (Avery et al., 2021; Berger, 2024). Introduction: Pelvic floor ultrasound has evolved over the past 2 decades from a predominantly anatomical imaging modality into a tool supporting functional assessment and rehabilitation. Its capability of visualizing pelvic floor structures in real time during contraction, relaxation, coughing, and straining has expanded its role beyond structural diagnosis and into physiotherapy practice. Aim: This narrative review aimed to examine the role of pelvic floor ultrasound in functional assessment and rehabilitation, with particular emphasis on ultrasound‑derived functional parameters and challenges related to standardization. Methods: Relevant literature was identified through searches of the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases, focusing on pelvic floor muscle function, rehabilitative ultrasound imaging, biofeedback, physiotherapy applications, and emerging ultrasound technologies. Results: Current evidence supports the transition of ultrasound from static anatomical imaging toward dynamic assessment of pelvic floor muscle performance. Commonly reported functional parameters include bladder neck mobility, pelvic floor elevation, levator hiatus dimensions, and hiatal reduction during contraction. Among these, levator hiatus dynamics appear to provide particularly meaningful information on the integrated mechanical effect of levator ani activation. Ultrasound may also support biofeedback, motor learning, individualized exercise instruction, and monitoring of treatment‑related changes. Emerging approaches, including shear‑wave elastography, automated image analysis, and artificial intelligence–assisted assessment, can make measurements less dependent on manual interpretation. Conclusions: Despite recent advances, functional pelvic floor ultrasound remains limited by heterogeneity in acquisition protocols, task instructions, outcome measures, and reporting methods. Future research should focus on consensus‑based protocols, core functional outcomes, structured reporting, and clinically meaningful reference values.
